root.name: Television, cassette drive and connectors

children.name: Why a television set was mandatory
children.description: The VIC-II chip outputs a 1 MHz-ish analogue composite signal on its own pin: luma, blanking and a colour subcarrier, but no RF. In 1982 there was no agreed analogue video standard between a computer and a monitor, no DE-15 or VGA, and no DVI. Commodore's answer was a small RF modulator, a printed board with one video modulator oscillator and a VHF converter, whose output was injected into the aerial socket of an ordinary television. The TV then had to be tuned to channel 3 (61.75 MHz in the US) or channel 4, and the picture was in colour only if the TV had a colour decoder for that subcarrier frequency.
inputs: composite video from the VIC-II pin

facts.label: Output impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm, unbalanced

facts.label: Output power
facts.value: roughly 0.5-1 mW (a few hundred microwatts to 1 milliwatt)

facts.label: Colour subcarrier
facts.value: 3.58 MHz (NTSC) / 4.43 MHz (PAL)

facts.label: Default channel
facts.value: channel 3 US, switchable to 4

children.note: The modulator board is usually treated as part of the C64, not as a peripheral, so it lives here as the hinge of this branch. Output power figures vary between sources; treat them as order-of-magnitude. A TV modulator injected at the aerial socket needs a floating (isolated) aerial input or the local TV signal will back-feed and wash out the computer picture, which is why sets with an isolated aerial socket were prized. The modulator itself is documented in the mainboard as mb.rf-modulator.

children.name: Domestic colour television set, 13 inch NTSC
children.description: A 1982-84 US domestic set: 12.5 or 13 inch diagonal, 525-line NTSC, 60 Hz field rate, all-signal-in-a-can. It was the only display a C64 owner was likely to have, and the C64 looked terrible on it: no separate chrominance bandwidth, a modulated sound carrier that carried the computer's audio, and a colour subcarrier at a frequency the TV's chroma band had to be tuned to.

facts.label: Picture tube diagonal
facts.value: 12.5 inch (318 mm) or 13 inch (330 mm); 19 inch sets were the other common size

facts.label: Field rate
facts.value: 60 Hz, 525 lines, 2:1 interlace

facts.label: Line rate
facts.value: 15,734 Hz (15,750 Hz nominal)

facts.label: EHT
facts.value: 20-25 kV, 1-2 mA total beam current

facts.label: Mains
facts.value: 117 V 60 Hz in the US, 240 V 50 Hz in Europe

children.note: The PAL/SECAM line rate is 12 kHz; NTSC is 15,734 Hz and every number on this branch is NTSC. 12.5 kHz is the line rate of the 50 Hz NTSC variants used in Japan and some export markets. Also worth stating plainly: there is no analogue TV transmitter here. A broadcast transmitter was a 100 kW-10 MW superstructure of tetrodes and a directional panel array; a home C64 needed a one-square-inch modulator board and a household set instead.

children.name: The picture tube (CRT)
children.description: A vacuum envelope of two pieces of glass welded together: a flat-ish panel carrying the phosphor screen inside its face, and a flanged funnel tapering to a cylindrical neck that carries the electron gun. The panel-to-funnel joint is sealed with a lead-oxide frit fired in a belt kiln. Inside the tube, electrons leave a hot cathode, are focused and accelerated to about 25 kV, steered magnetically across the panel, and slam into phosphor grains through a steel mask.

facts.label: Envelope volume
facts.value: roughly 5-8 litres, evacuated to better than 1e-6 mbar

facts.label: Envelope weight
facts.value: about 6-9 kg of glass for a 13 inch tube, roughly half of it the neck-adjacent cone

facts.label: Screen
facts.value: P22 phosphor, 3-colour dot triad

children.name: Faceplate panel and funnel, borosilicate glass
children.description: The tube is made of two glass parts that must expand at the same rate or the tube shatters at the seal. The funnel is a leaded or unlead borosilicate; the panel is a flatter, alkali-free glass with a much lower thermal expansion coefficient. Their junction is a strip of lead borosilicate frit, printed onto both parts and fired, which melts at a temperature low enough that the base glass does not slump.

facts.label: Panel glass
facts.value: about 2.5-3.1 mm thick, alkali-free borosilicate

facts.label: Funnel glass
facts.value: about 1.5-2.5 mm through the cone, flaring to 3-4 mm at the panel edge

facts.label: Frit border
facts.value: roughly 8-12 mm wide, 1-2 mm thick, all round the panel perimeter

facts.label: Frit firing
facts.value: devitrified at 600-700 degrees C, then belt-sealed to the funnel at 430-460 degrees C

children.note: A 24% PbO figure is what is usually quoted for the standard X-ray absorbing lead frit of the era, and it is representative rather than universal: real formulations ran from about a quarter to two thirds PbO depending on whether the set was sold as a colour tube with a separate shadow mask or a lower-cost monochrome-style lead frit.

children.name: P22 phosphor screen, blue/green/red
children.description: The inside face of the panel carries a printed tri-colour phosphor: blue zinc sulphide doped with silver, green zinc sulphide doped with gold, and a red phosphor around 610 nm, arranged as a dot triad maybe 0.6-0.8 mm pitch behind the shadow mask. The whole layer is only about 25-40 microns thick wet and shrinks to 15-25 microns fired, then gets a mirror of aluminium vapour on top so the electron beam that misses the phosphor is absorbed instead of lighting the room.

facts.label: Screen pitch
facts.value: 0.63-0.8 mm dot triad

facts.label: Blue
facts.value: ZnS:Ag, peak about 450-460 nm

facts.label: Green
facts.value: ZnS:Au (often with Cu or Sb), peak about 525 nm

facts.label: Red
facts.value: about 610 nm; formulations varied between CaS:Eu and Eu-doped ZnS

facts.label: Phosphor thickness
facts.value: 15-25 microns after firing

facts.label: Aluminium layer
facts.value: 0.1-0.5 microns, vapour deposited

children.note: The exact activator recipe for the red was proprietary and differed between manufacturers; the blue and green ZnS:Ag and ZnS:Au pair is the solid part of the P22 story. Blue ZnS:Ag is bandgap-limited emission from the ZnS host itself, the Ag is a co-activator that traps the electron, and Au in the green sits at a discrete level that emits 525 nm. A modern LCD has no phosphor at all.

children.name: Shadow mask and aperture grille
children.description: Without something to stop every beam landing on every phosphor, a CRT would be a monochrome tube with three faint colour washes. The shadow mask is a curved steel foil perforated with about 25,000 slots; the electron beam is steered so each of the three guns aims through the correct hole. The alternative is the aperture grille, two combs of tensioned vertical wires with no foil at all.

facts.label: Shadow mask pitch
facts.value: 0.63-0.8 mm slot pitch (0.63 mm typical, 0.8 mm on the wider-pitch sets of the early 80s)

facts.label: Vertical wires
facts.value: about 350-450 for a 13 inch tube at 0.63-0.8 mm pitch

facts.label: Mask material
facts.value: cold-reduced low-carbon steel strip, about 0.1-0.2 mm

children.note: A 0.6 mm slot pitch etched from 0.05 mm low-carbon steel is directionally right on pitch but the sheet gauge in practice was thicker than 0.05 mm. A mask at 0.05 mm would deflect itself into a catenary under its own weight during the 600 degree C stress relief; the industry used 0.1-0.2 mm cold-reduced low-carbon (1008) steel, and Sony's aperture-grille wires are about 0.12-0.15 mm diameter plated with nickel and chrome. 0.6 mm pitch is right for a 1982 set.

children.name: Aperture grille (Trinitron-type)
children.description: The alternative to a foil: two combs of vertical wires under tension, typically nickel-chrome plated steel wire, at a 0.5-0.6 mm pitch. Because the mask is vertical wires only, the beam can strike them from any horizontal position, which gives the Trinitron its famous vertically sharp picture and lets the two outer guns share a defocus. Two thin damper wires keep the combs from ringing.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 0.12-0.15 mm diameter, chrome plated

facts.label: Tension
facts.value: a few newtons, the combs are stressed by the frame

children.note: Sony's Trinitron was licensed to a handful of Japanese and European makers through the 1980s, so Trinitron-type tubes appeared in non-Sony sets too.

children.name: Electron gun, three guns
children.description: Three parallel electron guns in one pinch, one per phosphor, each with a hot cathode, a control grid, a screen grid, a focus grid and an anode. In a 13 inch set of 1982 they were usually separate but adjacent, converging at the screen; the convergence magnets on the neck bent them into line and the electrostatic or magnetic focus brought the three spot sizes down to about 0.5-1.0 mm at the panel.

facts.label: Heater voltage
facts.value: 6.3 V per gun at about 0.6-0.9 A each, all three in parallel off a flyback auxiliary winding

facts.label: Filament temperature
facts.value: 2400-2600 degrees C

facts.label: Cathode-1st anode voltage
facts.value: about 400-700 V

facts.label: Spot size at panel
facts.value: 0.5-1.0 mm at the centre of screen

children.name: Oxide-coated cathode, Ba-Sr-Ca on nickel-chromium
children.description: A cup-shaped nickel-chromium alloy base, sprayed with barium, strontium and calcium carbonates fired to oxides, with a caesium or platinum-tantalum dispenser. The oxides are a thermionic emitter: work function about 2 eV against 4.5 eV for tungsten, which is why a cathode runs at 750-850 degrees C while a tungsten filament runs at 2500.

facts.label: Emission
facts.value: work function about 2.0-2.6 eV

facts.label: Operating temperature
facts.value: 730-850 degrees C

facts.label: Lifetime
facts.value: 10,000-30,000 hours in a small set

children.note: The cathode is one of the few parts of a television that is a genuine consumable with a finite life, and its end-of-life symptom was a dim, discoloured picture that a serviceman could fix with a gun rejuvenator that momentarily pushed the heater voltage far above rating. The barium, strontium and calcium that form the coating come from one alkaline-earth mining chain that served three different parts of the same set - this coating, the speaker ferrite and the barium getter in the neck - which is a convergence worth seeing rather than repeating.

children.name: Tungsten heater filament
children.description: A hair-fine tungsten wire folded into a flat zig-zag under the cathode cup and buried in its oxides. Typical wire 0.04-0.08 mm diameter, 60-150 mm long, running at 6.3 V. It is the only hot tungsten in the gun and by far the largest source of tube failure.

facts.label: Melting point of W
facts.value: 3422 degrees C

children.note: Tungsten has the highest melting point of all known elements, at 3,422 C, and is used in incandescent lamp filaments. Not established: the 0.04-0.08 mm wire diameter, the 60-150 mm length, and the claim that this filament is by far the largest source of tube failure.

children.name: Focus and screen grids, nickel sheet
children.description: The grid stack is a set of thin nickel foils laser-welded or spot-welded into a unit: G1 the Wehnelt and video modulator, G2 the screen grid at a few hundred volts, G3 the focus grid at 5-20% of the anode voltage, and the anode block itself in graphite or aluminium with a ceramic or mica spacer stack. Every surface is blackened.

facts.label: G1
facts.value: Wehnelt and video, a few volts negative to cathode

facts.label: G3 focus grid
facts.value: 1-5 kV on a small set

facts.label: Spacers
facts.value: alumina ceramic, spot-welded

children.note: An electron gun is built from a cathode and a stack of biased grids that shape and focus the beam, and that much is documented. Not established: that the grids were nickel sheet, that the stack was laser welded rather than spot welded (spot welding of nickel grid stacks was the normal joining method and laser welding of grids is a later technique), the alumina ceramic spot-welded spacers, the 400-800 V screen grid, the 1-5 kV focus grid on a small set, the graphite or aluminium anode block, and the nickel-zinc ferrite slug on the neck if one was fitted. The three-grid voltages given are plausible for a small set but no service data for a 1982 tube was consulted for them.

children.name: Static focus coil on the neck
children.description: On the cheaper sets the three guns were focused by one small coil slipped over the neck outside the vacuum envelope, adjustable from the back of the set. Sets without static focus simply ran the focus grid at a fixed voltage and adjusted focus only for the corners with a convergence adjustment in the yoke.

facts.label: Field
facts.value: a few hundred gauss in a short air-core solenoid

children.note: Static focus coils were common in small sets of the early 80s and largely disappeared as focus went entirely electrostatic.
Not established: the 6.3 V at 0.6-0.9 A per gun heater supply, the 2400-2600 C filament temperature, the 400-700 V cathode-first-anode voltage, and the 0.5-1.0 mm spot size at the centre of screen.

children.name: Deflection yoke and deflection coils
children.description: A bell-shaped ferrite or powdered-iron core clamped on the tube neck carrying two orthogonal saddle windings. The horizontal winding is driven by the line output stage and sits in series with the flyback, so the scan current is the same current that steps up to 25 kV. The vertical winding is in the collector of the vertical output stage and carries a sawtooth at 60 Hz.

facts.label: Deflection angle
facts.value: 90 degrees typical, 100 degrees on the higher-power sets

facts.label: Horizontal scan current
facts.value: 1-2 A peak to peak

facts.label: Vertical scan current
facts.value: 0.2-0.8 A peak to peak

facts.label: Deflection
facts.value: about 8-9 mm peak in the horizontal direction on a 13 inch tube

facts.label: Pincushion correction
facts.value: pins and a C-core on the yoke, or electronic linearity in the line stage

children.name: Enamelled copper winding, single harness
children.description: Copper wire, 0.2-0.4 mm, enamel-insulated and wound onto a bobbin with the horizontal coils outside and the vertical coils inside, then immersed in epoxy or polyurethane varnish to lock the winding rigidly. The hum-cancelling trick on the read head of a cassette deck has an ancestor here: the horizontal coils are arranged so their fields oppose.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 0.2-0.4 mm, and the hum-bucking deflection coils use bifilar or twisted pairs

children.name: Glass-filled nylon bobbin
children.description: Yoke bobbins and coil formers were glass-filled nylon (PA66-GF30) because the winding runs hot and phenolic would crack. Nylon 6,6 comes from adipic acid plus hexamethylenediamine, both from petroleum.

facts.label: Resin
facts.value: PA66, glass filled to 30% for stiffness above 150 degrees C

children.note: Nylon 66 is a documented engineering thermoplastic, and a glass-filled grade of a thermoplastic is a normal coil former material where heat and mechanical strength both matter. Not established: that the bobbin was specifically PA66 rather than glass-filled PET, PBT or phenolic, the 30% chopped E-glass loading, the figure of about 150 C for the stiffness the glass fill buys, and the claim that phenolic would have cracked on a hot winding. Nylon 66 is also the material this file gives the cassette hub, which is the better-evidenced of the two uses; the coil former and the hub are different parts and are not evidence for each other.

Magnet wire and enamelled copper wire are documented as the normal way a deflection coil is wound. Not established: the 0.2-0.4 mm wire gauge, bifilar or twisted-pair winding in the hum-bucking coils, epoxy or polyurethane immersion varnish, and the specific coil nesting of horizontals outside and verticals inside. The link drawn here between the opposed horizontal coils and the hum-cancelling head winding of a cassette deck is a design analogy, not a documented shared lineage; the head winding is documented on its own node, and nothing consulted says the yoke coil was wound to cancel mains hum.

children.name: Conicity and geometry correction magnets
children.description: A 13 inch set with a 90 degree deflection had visible pincushion and barrel distortion. Correction was partly mechanical: a pair of small magnets on the neck that tilted the field to change the deflection centre, a static C-core for pincushion, and inside the flyback a 'geometry' winding that shapes the scan current. The customer-facing result was a V-hold, H-hold, width, height, linearity and convergence control on the back of the chassis, and on a cheap set a bright-line adjustment they could get wrong.
children.note: Electronic pincushion correction using a diode and capacitor in the line stage was common from the mid 1970s; the amount varies by set.
Not established: the 90 degree typical deflection angle and 100 degree higher-power figure, the 1-2 A horizontal and 0.2-0.8 A vertical scan currents, and the 8-9 mm scan on a 13 inch tube.

children.name: EHT / line output transformer (flyback)
children.description: The flyback does three jobs at once: it steps the 120 V B+ up to 20-25 kV for the anode, it develops the high flyback pulse that the line output transistor uses to make its collector current fall fast, and it carries auxiliary windings that supply the 12-25 V the gun heater, the tuner motor, the oscillator and the horizontal oscillator circuits need. In 1982 it was an open-frame transformer on a laminated or ferrite core, wrapped in epoxy and varnished, mounted on the chassis next to the tube neck with several hundred volts between it and everything else.

facts.label: Primary voltage
facts.value: about 120 V B+, switched at 15,734 Hz

facts.label: HV output
facts.value: 20-25 kV DC, 1-2 mA

facts.label: Turns ratio
facts.value: roughly 1:200 to the HV winding

facts.label: HV wire
facts.value: 0.03-0.05 mm enamelled copper, 10,000-25,000 turns

facts.label: Flyback pulse
facts.value: 150-350 V above B+, for 5-15 microseconds

facts.label: Insulation
facts.value: epoxy and mylar, rated for a 1 kV test

children.note: A line output swinging about 1 kV across the yoke is the figure for a large 25 inch set with a 110 degree tube and a high line current. On a 13 inch set with a 90 degree deflection the yoke current is of the order of 1-2 A peak to peak into a few tens of ohms, so the voltage across the yoke is tens to a couple of hundred volts, and the flyback still steps it to 20-25 kV. The 1 kV figure is also sometimes quoted as the voltage on the yoke during retrace once the damper is included.

children.name: Silicon EHT rectifier diode
children.description: A single high-voltage silicon diode, or a small stack of them, rated 3-10 kV reverse and 1-5 mA forward, potted in silicone rubber or epoxy so the 25 kV does not arc. The cathode end of the HV winding goes to the rectifier and the anode to the tube's anode terminal. A set with a failing EHT rectifier was a common and unpleasant repair.

facts.label: Reverse rating
facts.value: 3-10 kV silicon, or a 2-3 diode stack

facts.label: Forward current
facts.value: 1-5 mA

facts.label: Potting
facts.value: silicone rubber or epoxy, rated for the full EHT

children.note: A silicon rectifier diode as the single element that turns the flyback high-voltage pulses into the DC anode supply is the standard arrangement in that generation of sets. Not established: the 3-10 kV reverse rating and the 1-5 mA forward current as 1982 values, the two or three diode stack as an alternative, silicone rubber or epoxy potting rated for the full EHT, and the claim that a failing EHT rectifier was a common and unpleasant repair. The fault mode is certainly real, because the rectifier is the component that sees the full anode voltage; its frequency as a service complaint is not documented. High-voltage silicon rectifiers with forward currents of a few milliamperes are a long-established product class, so the order of magnitude here is defensible.

children.name: Anode terminal: the lead burned through the funnel wall
children.description: The EHT gets into the tube through a metal button, usually a nickel or Kovar cup, sealed into the funnel wall with a glass frit and then fired. Above that terminal sits a silicone-rubber-covered anode cap that had to survive being touched with a screwdriver in a live set. A rubber anode cap failing was a genuine fire and electrocution hazard, and the safety information people remember about 1970s-80s TVs comes from exactly this part.

facts.label: Terminal
facts.value: nickel or Kovar button frit-sealed into the funnel wall at 430-460 degrees C

facts.label: External cap
facts.value: silicone rubber, 3-6 mm of insulation

facts.label: Voltage
facts.value: 20-25 kV DC at this terminal

children.note: The internal portion of the anode button was itself the visible example of a glass-to-metal seal, and was where most early implosion-protection advertising pointed. Not established: the nickel or Kovar button frit-sealed at 430-460 C, the 3-6 mm silicone cap, and the 20-25 kV figure at this terminal.

children.name: Implosion protection and the safety faceplate
children.description: A colour TV tube holds about 0.5-1.5 tonnes per square metre of glass at a quarter atmosphere, and shatters into shards that will cut. Three defences: a laminate or thicker-than-necessary faceplate whose edges are the thickest part, a mask retaining ring that holds the faceplate to the frame rather than letting it come out, and a wraparound rim so the panel cannot pop forward. Cheap sets used less glass; expensive and safe sets used a tempered or laminated panel and, from the late 1970s, an implosion protection plate bonded to the front.

facts.label: Pressure
facts.value: about 0.2-0.3 bar differential (a partial vacuum, not a hard vacuum, by design)

facts.label: Front glass
facts.value: 3-6 mm, often laminated or bonded to an implosion plate

facts.label: Rim
facts.value: wraparound steel or plastic retaining ring

children.note: The pressure figure needs care. A TV tube is evacuated to high vacuum, but the internal volume is large and the glass is thick enough that the tube is deliberately designed so that a manufacturing flaw (a large void or a heavy impurity in the glass) is a slow leak, not a bomb. Post-deflection the tube may be brought back to a small positive pressure by letting in a little inert gas; the net differential is around a fifth of an atmosphere, not one atmosphere. That is a large fraction of the energy a naive reader would assume, and it is the reason the safety story is not simply 'it is a vacuum bomb'.

children.name: RF tuner, VHF and UHF
children.description: The front end. In 1982 the US TV band was VHF channels 2-13 (55-220 MHz) and UHF 14-83 (470-890 MHz), and most sets had either a combined tuner or two side-by-side ones behind a single dial. A high-quality set used a rotary switch with a chain of interlocking contacts; a cheap one used a varactor diode and a small motor, or a continuous mechanical tuning with a motor and a rotor. Whatever the mechanism, the output was always the same: a fixed 45 MHz intermediate frequency.

facts.label: VHF band
facts.value: channels 2-13, 54-216 MHz

facts.label: UHF band
facts.value: channels 14-83, 470-890 MHz

facts.label: IF output
facts.value: 45.0 MHz centre

facts.label: IF carriers
facts.value: picture 45.75 MHz, colour 42.47 MHz, sound 54.75 MHz

facts.label: Input impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm, unbalanced

children.note: A 4-gang tuner, separate RF and mixer coils for both bands in one switch, was the older high-quality approach; by 1982 varactor tuning with a motor and AFC was increasingly common, and a mechanical rotary tuner with a 4-gang arrangement was still on plenty of sets.

children.name: VHF gangs: RF amplifier and mixer coils
children.description: Two tuned circuits on ferrite cores: an RF amplifier and a mixer, both switched through a gang so they track. The coils are a few turns of enamelled copper on ferrite slug cores; the switch has a rotor with printed or wound inductors that tap through the band, and an AFC or motor to pull it into lock.

facts.label: Band
facts.value: 54-216 MHz, four switched ranges in older sets

facts.label: Core
facts.value: nickel-zinc ferrite, tunable with a ferrite slug

children.note: A tuner is documented as the component that selects one wanted signal from the antenna feed, and the intermediate frequency stage downstream of the mixer is documented separately. Two switched tuned circuits on ferrite slug cores, tracking through a gang, is the standard VHF tuner arrangement of the period. Not established: 54-216 MHz as the band with four switched ranges, the 45 MHz sound IF and the picture IF implied by the switch contacts, nickel-zinc ferrite as the slug material, a rotor carrying printed or wound inductors to tap through the band, and the AFC or motor tuning. The frequency ranges and the IF figures are the ones that vary by market and standard and would need a service manual for the set in question.

children.name: UHF tuner with varactor diode
children.description: At 500-800 MHz a lumped LC circuit is hopeless, so the UHF tuner used a coaxial cavity or a stripline distributed resonator made of folded sheet metal, with a silicon varactor diode as the tuning element. Reverse-biasing the diode changed its junction capacitance from tens to a few picofarads, which moved the resonance across the band. A small DC motor rotated the cavity to track, or a servo pushed a varactor.

facts.label: Varactor capacitance
facts.value: about 3-20 pF at the bias range, changing with reverse voltage

facts.label: Cavity
facts.value: folded-sheet transmission line, about 10-20 mm across

facts.label: Tuning motor
facts.value: a small DC gearmotor with a plastic cam, 12-24 V

children.name: Varactor diode, silicon planar junction
children.description: A reverse-biased silicon pn junction used as a voltage-variable capacitor. At zero bias the depletion layer is thin and the capacitance is at its maximum; raising the reverse voltage widens the depletion layer and drops the capacitance. The diode is a small pill or a leaded axial part soldered into the cavity wall, and the DC bias arrives through a high-value resistor from the tuner supply.

facts.label: Capacitance ratio
facts.value: about 4:1 across the band

facts.label: Bias
facts.value: 5-30 V reverse

children.note: Silicon varactors, and later the whole family of PIN diodes used for AGC and trap switching, were the reason TV tuners had a whole discrete semiconductor family of their own in the 1980s.

children.name: Cavity resonator, brass or nickel-plated steel
children.description: The UHF resonant circuit is a piece of metal: folded sheet or machined brass forming a half-wavelength line, with the shunt capacitance of the varactor at the open end and a tap for the transistor. This is one of the few places in a television where the RF circuit is metal rather than a PCB, because at 800 MHz a printed board would radiate. Brass came from zinc and copper ores.
inputs: silver plating on the contact fingers
children.note: No source was found for this construction. At UHF a printed board is generally abandoned in favour of a distributed resonator, so the metal cavity is the right kind of answer and the reasoning about radiation is sound. Not established: that the cavity was folded sheet or machined brass rather than nickel-plated steel or a die-cast zinc shell, the half-wavelength line dimension, the varactor mounted as a shunt capacitance across the open end, the tap for the transistor, and the silver plating on the contact fingers. The brass-to-copper-and-zinc statement at the end is correct as an alloy statement but the zinc it names is the zinc of a connector body, not necessarily of this cavity.

A varactor diode is documented: it is designed to exploit the voltage-dependent capacitance of a reverse-biased p-n junction, no DC current flows in that state, and varactors are used in the frequency synthesizers that tune radios, television sets and cellular telephones. That establishes the tuning element. Not established: that this 1982 set used a varactor rather than a mechanically rotated cavity, the 3-20 pF capacitance range, the 10-20 mm cavity dimension, the 12-24 V gearmotor with a plastic cam, and whether tuning was motorised, switched or by a rotating core. UHF tuners of the period used all three approaches, and which one a given set had is a service-manual detail.

children.name: RF amplifier and mixer
children.description: A low-noise bipolar or MOSFET amplifier at the antenna frequency, then a mixer down to 45 MHz. In 1982 the RF device was often a silicon planar MOSFET (dual-gate, for the UHF) or a wideband bipolar. The whole RF section lived in a die-cast or stamped zinc-plated steel can to keep it away from the switching supply and the line output.

children.name: SAW filter at 45 MHz
children.description: By the early 1980s a SAW (surface acoustic wave) filter had largely replaced the LC or ceramic filter in the IF path. Two interdigital transducers on a piezoelectric crystal launch and pick up an acoustic wave along the surface; the finger pattern is designed to pass the wanted band and reject the adjacent channel, sound and colour carriers. It gave a picture with no intermodulation and no cross modulation between the picture, colour and sound carriers.

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: 40-cut Y-cut lithium niobate, or lithium tantalate

facts.label: Centre frequency
facts.value: 45.0 MHz, bandwidth about 6 MHz

facts.label: Electrodes
facts.value: photolithographically deposited aluminium, about 100-200 nm

facts.label: Insertion loss
facts.value: 1-3 dB

children.note: Not established: the silicon planar dual-gate MOSFET as the 1982 UHF RF device, and the 45 MHz mixer output.

children.name: Die-cast zinc or stamped steel RF can
children.description: The tuner and front end were a sealed metal can soldered to the main board. On a cheap set it was a stamped zinc-plated steel can; on a good one a die-cast zinc or aluminium can with a machined seam. Zinc plating comes from zinc electroplating baths, so it is the same zinc industry as the galvanised chassis.
inputs: zinc-plated sheet steel or die-cast zinc
children.note: Zinc die-casting was one of the biggest single uses of zinc in 1982, far larger than the CRT frit. A zinc-plated steel can is also a small, forgotten consumer of zinc alongside the chassis and the screws.

children.name: Dial cord and pulley gear train
children.description: The channel knob turned a pulley that wound a braided cord onto another pulley geared to the tuner rotor. It was a real mechanical system that stretched, slipped and broke, and it is the reason every vintage-TV owner has a drawer of spare dial cords. The cord was a braided polyester or nylon sheath over a cotton core.
children.note: The polyester dial cord is the same base polymer as the tape leader and the oven bag: PET again. Not established: the braided polyester or nylon sheath over a cotton core, and the geared pulley between the channel knob and the tuner rotor.

children.name: The chassis: video, sync, line output, audio
children.description: The electronics of the set. By 1982 this was a single-sided or double-sided printed circuit board carrying a mix of discrete transistors, a handful of silicon integrated circuits (the video amplifier, the chroma, the vertical, the audio), a rotary switch bank and about forty electrolytic and film capacitors. The board sat in a zinc-plated steel chassis with a perforated steel cover, and the flyback sat beside it throwing both heat and electromagnetic noise.

facts.label: Board
facts.value: FR-4 epoxy-glass laminate, single-sided in a cheap set

facts.label: Power input
facts.value: B+ rail about 115-120 V from a linear supply, or a small switcher

facts.label: Colour decoder
facts.value: NTSC quadrature demodulator with a phase-locked multiply

facts.label: Audio
facts.value: 4.5 MHz intercarrier FM

children.name: FR-4 epoxy-glass printed circuit board
children.description: Glass-reinforced epoxy laminate with a copper foil laminated to each side and printed photolithographically. The glass fibre is the reason FR-4 has a low, controlled thermal expansion; the epoxy binds it. It is drilled, plated through with copper, mask-printed and silkscreened. After etching, the whole board is flooded with a green or brown epoxy solder mask about 10-25 microns thick, leaving only the pads open, and white epoxy legend ink is silkscreened through a fine mesh for the reference designators. The mask is itself an epoxy, and the legend is a screen-printable ink cured rather than melted. Mask is printed before the tin-lead dip, so it covers the copper that the dip is going to throw away.

facts.label: Copper foil
facts.value: 35 micrometres, electrolytic

facts.label: Glass content
facts.value: about 60% by weight E-glass

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: FR-4, Tg about 130-140 degrees C

facts.label: Solder mask
facts.value: epoxy, 10-25 microns, over everything but the pads

facts.label: Legend
facts.value: one or two passes of white epoxy ink through a silkscreen mesh

children.note: Colour sets of the period were green or brown-black; the tan-and-brown Tiger FR-4 everyone associates with the era was common but not universal.

children.name: Video chain: IF, detector, video amp, colour
children.description: The 45 MHz IF is amplified, limited, then detected: the video signal rides on the picture carrier at 45.75 MHz, the colour subcarrier sits 3.58 MHz below it as a sideband, and the sound carrier sits 9 MHz above at 54.75 MHz. The synchronous detector recovers the baseband video; a PLL multiplies the recovered 3.58 MHz subcarrier up and phase-shifts it 90 degrees to drive the two demodulators; the result is U and V, added back to luminance to give R, G and B, which drive the gun cathodes.

facts.label: Detectors
facts.value: synchronous (PLL multiplier) in a good set, envelope plus a Reinschmidt envelope detector in a cheap one

facts.label: Video bandwidth
facts.value: 4.5 MHz (-3 dB), so the 3.58 MHz colour subcarrier is attenuated at the picture edges

facts.label: Colour demodulation
facts.value: quadrature, 90 degrees apart, PLL recovered subcarrier

facts.label: IF gain
facts.value: 60-70 dB total across three to five stages

children.note: The video bandwidth of 4.5 MHz is why a C64's 320x200 pixels, drawn as a very narrow TV line, showed colour fringes and lost horizontal resolution on a set with no notch filter. A set with a notch filter and a comb filter, common on 1980s sets, recovered much of it. The 'quality' switch on a late-70s set simply inserted a notch at the colour subcarrier. Not established: the 45.75 MHz picture carrier, the 3.58 MHz colour subcarrier, the 4.5 MHz video bandwidth and the 60-70 dB IF gain as this set's values.

children.name: Silicon integrated circuit, 4-micron NMOS
children.description: The video, chroma and audio functions in a 1982 set were often one or two chips of 40 to 80 pins, made on a 4-5 micron NMOS or bipolar process. The die is a slice of 99.99% silicon, oxidised, photolithographically patterned through eight to ten mask steps, and packaged in epoxy or ceramic. Purity, oxide quality and aluminium interconnect over a polysilicon gate is the whole story of the 4-micron generation.

facts.label: Feature size
facts.value: 4-5 micron minimum line, 8-10 masks

facts.label: Die
facts.value: about 3-5 mm square

facts.label: Package
facts.value: plastic DIP, epoxy mould

children.note: The integrated circuit is documented as a compact assembly of electronic circuits fabricated onto a thin flat piece of semiconductor material, most commonly silicon, integrated circuits are integral to a wide variety of electronic devices including televisions, its three advantages over discrete components are size, cost and performance because the components are printed as a unit by photolithography rather than being constructed one transistor at a time, and the main disadvantage is the high initial design cost. That is the right framework for a 1982 video and chroma chip. Not established: that video, chroma and audio sat on one or two chips of 40 to 80 pins in a 1982 set, the 4-5 micron NMOS minimum line and 8-10 mask steps, the 3-5 mm die, the polysilicon-gate claim for that generation (an aluminium gate on polysilicon is a later generation than 1982), and the Santa Clara, Dallas and Tokyo works. The comment that this is what the C64 analogue chain also used is a comparison, not a shared sourcing record.

children.name: Discrete IF, driver and video transistors
children.description: Most transistors in a 1982 set were discrete: a high-gain IF transistor, the video driver, the video output transistors, the horizontal oscillator and driver, the vertical output, the audio output, and the horizontal output. Each is a tiny die, 10-40 transistors, wire-bonded to a plastic or metal can. Metal-can transistors (TO-18) were still common in the IF and video stages where heat and shielding mattered.

facts.label: Count
facts.value: 30-80 discrete transistors per set

facts.label: Packages
facts.value: TO-92 plastic, TO-18 metal can, TO-3 or a plastic power package for the audio and line output

facts.label: Bipolar
facts.value: mostly NPN small-signal, gain-bandwidth product 100 MHz to a few GHz

children.name: The transistor die and its package
children.description: A small-signal NPN transistor is a few hundred square microns of silicon, aluminium metallised, mounted on a header and sealed in epoxy or metal. The die itself is a slice of the same 99.99% wafer as the video IC, cut with a diamond-impregnated wheel and diced on a saw.

facts.label: Die size
facts.value: a few hundred square microns to about 1 mm square

facts.label: Beta
facts.value: 100-400 for a small-signal IF or video transistor

facts.label: fT
facts.value: 100 MHz to a few GHz

children.note: No independent source for the figures here. The mechanism described is documented on the integrated circuit itself: the components are printed as a unit by photolithography onto a thin flat piece of semiconductor material rather than being constructed one transistor at a time. What that source does not give is the geometry of a discrete small-signal die. Not established: the die area of a few hundred square microns to about 1 mm2, the beta of 100-400 for an IF or video transistor, the gain-bandwidth figures as 1982 values, the diamond-impregnated wheel cut, and the Santa Clara, Tokyo and Taipei works. A die a few hundred microns square with ten to forty transistors is a plausible reconstruction of what a TO-92 small-signal part contains, but no datasheet for a 1982 television transistor was consulted.

A bipolar junction transistor is documented: it uses two p-n junctions between n-type and p-type regions of one crystal so that a small current injected at one terminal controls a much larger current between the other two, and hundreds can be made on one circuit at very low cost. The discrete-transistor set is coherent. Not established: 30-80 discrete transistors per set, that TO-18 metal-can packages were still common in the IF and video stages in 1982 (TO-92 had taken over most small-signal sockets by then, and metal cans went mainly to low-noise and high-voltage roles), the 10-40 transistor die, the gain-bandwidth range as a 1982 figure, and that the video, chroma and audio functions were discrete at all rather than integrated, which is the premise of the sibling video chip node.

children.name: Automatic gain control
children.description: The AGC samples the DC level off the video detector and feeds a reverse bias back to the first two IF stages, holding the picture bright whether the aerial is good or the C64 modulator is a milliwatt away from nothing. This was the one part of a TV that genuinely cared about the C64 signal, because a C64 was a much weaker source than a broadcast station and the AGC had to find a way to open up. A key-operated AGC defeat, or a 'manual gain' switch, was a modification for fringe-area reception.
children.note: In a set of this vintage the AGC was a discrete little circuit block with its own transistors and its own fault symptom - a dim, over-driven picture when fed from a milliwatt modulator - and it was the one stage a user or a serviceman actually touched with a screwdriver. A circuit block is a thing you can point at on a board.

children.name: Horizontal line output stage, 15,734 Hz
children.description: The heart of the set's power and geometry. The line oscillator runs at 15,734 Hz; the driver and the output transistor switch the flyback primary, so the collector current rises linearly during scan and then collapses in the flyback retrace. The flyback uses that collapse to develop a high-voltage pulse, rectified to the EHT. The same transformer runs back through the damper to create a 200-250 V pump rail for the video output stage. In 1982 this was usually a discrete silicon EFT (a triple-diffused or a high-voltage epitaxial transistor) because a single silicon transistor could not safely switch a 900 V collector at 15.7 kHz.

facts.label: Output transistor
facts.value: silicon EFT, 600-1000 V Vce, 5-15 A peak, 400-1000 W peak pulse

facts.label: Flyback pulse
facts.value: 150-350 V above B+, for 5-15 microseconds, every line

facts.label: Pump rail
facts.value: 200-250 V DC from the damper and a rectifier

children.note: A 12 kHz line rate is the PAL figure. NTSC is 15,734 Hz, and a 13 inch US set of 1982 is a 15.7 kHz machine. A 1 kV swing across the yoke is a large-set number.

children.name: Line oscillator and AFC
children.description: A free-running LC oscillator locked to the incoming video by a sync separator and an automatic frequency control loop. When the set was fed a C64 signal it was free-running off the internal oscillator and being pulled by the modulator's sync; it could not lock to a broadcast, so it did not drift. Most of the visible misbehaviour of a C64 on a TV (rolling, tearing, drifting) came from this loop or from the modulator's own sync, not from the computer.

facts.label: Hold range
facts.value: several kHz either side of 15,734 Hz

facts.label: V-hold
facts.value: a control that shifts the vertical frequency to stop the picture rolling

children.note: Not established: the 15,734 Hz line frequency and the several-kilohertz AFC hold range. That a free-running oscillator is pulled by the modulator's sync and could not lock to a broadcast is the reliable part.

children.name: Line choke or choke-and-flyback combination
children.description: Some sets had a separate choke, some combined the choke with the flyback into one transformer. The choke carries the DC component of the line current and presents a high impedance to the 15.7 kHz pulse. It was an iron-powder or ferrite part with a thousand volts across it and was a common failure.

facts.label: Inductance
facts.value: a few hundred microhenries at 15.7 kHz

facts.label: Voltage
facts.value: hundreds of volts of pulse

children.note: The 13 inch sets of the early 1980s more often used a separate flyback with a discrete line choke; the integrated choke-and-flyback became common in the mid 1980s.

children.name: EHT rectifier and capacitor
children.description: After the flyback, a single silicon rectifier at 25 kV. On larger sets a doubler or tripler with plastic film capacitors at 2-5 kV each was used. The current was tiny (1-2 mA) so the capacitors were small in value but enormous in voltage rating, and their failure mode was spectacular and occasionally violent.

facts.label: Voltage
facts.value: 20-25 kV DC

facts.label: Capacitors
facts.value: 0.1-1 microfarad film at 2-5 kV each, in a doubler or tripler

facts.label: Failure
facts.value: a shorted film cap can throw the rectifier and the flyback

children.note: The flyback is documented as a line output transformer generating high-voltage sawtooth signals and used for outputs over 10 kV, which is the arrangement this node describes downstream of it. Not established: 20-25 kV DC as the anode supply of a 1982 set (tube screen sizes and standards set this, and it is a per-set figure), the 0.1-1 microfarad film capacitance at 2-5 kV per unit, the doubler or tripler topology, and the claim that a shorted film capacitor could throw both the rectifier and the flyback. A rectifier and a set of series capacitors is the standard single-ended EHT arrangement, so the topology is sound; the component values are not sourced.

children.name: High-voltage film capacitor
children.description: A metallised polypropylene or polystyrene film capacitor rated at kilovolts. The film is stretched polypropylene, metallised with a thin aluminium or zinc layer, wound, and the whole thing impregnated and potted. Zinc metallising was cheap and equivalent to aluminium for small values; aluminium became standard for reliability.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 2-5 kV DC continuous

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: metallised polypropylene or metallised polystyrene

children.note: Metallized film is documented as polymer plastic film coated with a thin layer of metal, usually aluminium, used for specialty applications including electronics. Polypropylene is documented as a thermoplastic of the polyolefin group, partially crystalline and non-polar, slightly harder and more heat-resistant than polyethylene, and the second most widely produced commodity plastic after polyethylene. Not established: that either polymer was the dielectric in this position, the 2-5 kV DC continuous rating for a 1982 television EHT capacitor, polystyrene as an alternative dielectric here (polystyrene film was largely displaced by polypropylene in mains and pulse capacitors because of its dielectric loss and its temperature coefficient, so it is a poor choice at kilovolt pulse duty), zinc metallising as the cheap alternative to aluminium, and epoxy potting as standard. The self-healing mechanism is a real property of metallised film, but it is stated on the neighbouring mains capacitor rather than repeated here.

children.name: Vertical output stage, 60 Hz
children.description: The vertical sweep at 60 Hz. The oscillator ran at twice the line rate and a count-down circuit divided by two, a design that keeps the vertical locked to the horizontal. The output stage amplified a small ramp and drove the vertical yoke, with a small electrolytic capacitor across the coil to correct the crosstalk that coupling into the horizontal yoke produced. A IC did most of this, with one or two power transistors at the output.

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: 60 Hz field, 31.5 kHz oscillator (2x line)

facts.label: Sweep
facts.value: about 12-16 mm peak to peak

facts.label: Output
facts.value: 0.2-0.8 A peak to peak

children.name: Vertical IC
children.description: A single IC contained the oscillator, the count-down divider, the ramp generator and the driver, needing only two or three external transistors. It was one of the first large consumer uses of a mixed-analogue IC that made a television much easier to build, and it is the reason a 1982 TV was a single-board affair.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: oscillator, divider, ramp, driver in one 16-20 pin package

children.note: By the mid-1980s these verticals had integrated the whole deflection drive on to one chip including the line output; that trend began here.
Not established: the 60 Hz field rate, the 31.5 kHz oscillator at twice line rate, the 12-16 mm sweep and the 0.2-0.8 A output as figures for a specific set.

children.name: Audio: 4.5 MHz intercarrier to a speaker
children.description: The sound carrier is taken off the same IF strip at 54.75 MHz, recovered at 4.5 MHz above the video, limited and FM-demodulated, then amplified. The 4.5 MHz intercarrier was chosen so the sound did not interfere with the video and to let the sound survive a picture cut-off (the 'intercarrier' idea). Amplified to a few watts into an 8 ohm speaker, or about 2 W per speaker into two 8 ohm speakers in parallel. The C64's audio came out of this amplifier, which is why it was loud, thin and slightly buzzy.

facts.label: Sound carrier
facts.value: 54.75 MHz IF, 4.5 MHz intercarrier, 75 kHz deviation, 15 kHz max audio

facts.label: Detector
facts.value: quadrature FM or a Foster-Seeley / ratio detector, sometimes with a limiter

facts.label: Output
facts.value: 2-5 W into 8 ohm; stereo sets about 2 W per side

facts.label: Audio bandwidth
facts.value: about 200 Hz to 8-10 kHz on a small set

children.note: The 75 kHz deviation and 15 kHz maximum audio are the NTSC TV audio figures. PAL/SECAM used 50 kHz deviation and a 6.5 MHz intercarrier for stereo, which is why PAL sets used a sound trap filter and NTSC sets used a notch. Not established: the 54.75 MHz sound IF, the 4.5 MHz intercarrier, the 75 kHz deviation and the 15 kHz maximum audio as this set's figures. The PAL and SECAM contrast in the note is right in outline but is not documented here either.

children.name: Intercarrier sound trap and SAW filter
children.description: The 4.5 MHz intercarrier has to be lifted out of the video baseband without disturbing the 3.58 MHz colour subcarrier, so a trap or SAW filter at 4.5 MHz ran between the video detector and the audio detector. A ceramic or SAW trap on 4.5 MHz was a very visible part in a 1982 set.
children.note: Not established: a 4.5 MHz ceramic or SAW trap between the video detector and the audio detector as 1982 practice, and the 3.58 MHz colour subcarrier in that role.

children.name: Audio output amplifier
children.description: An integrated amplifier (a few watts, a single 8-14 pin IC) or a discrete predriver plus two complementary power transistors pushing 5-20 W peak into 8 ohms from a 115 V rail. The output stage ran in class B or class AB, and the bias and the idle current were the main design problem.

facts.label: Power
facts.value: 2-5 W rms at 8 ohm from about 15-25 V DC

facts.label: Devices
facts.value: complementary NPN/PNP silicon pair, TO-3 or a plastic power package

children.name: The output power transistor
children.description: The device that actually pushed the current into the speaker: an NPN/PNP complementary pair on a thick die in a TO-3 or plastic power package, bolted to the chassis as its own heatsink. From 1990s multisilicon dice replaced the single-crystal die, but a 1982 set had one transistor per output channel.
inputs: TO-3 can with a beryllium oxide or mica isolator

facts.label: Output
facts.value: 5-20 W peak from a 20-40 V rail

facts.label: Package
facts.value: TO-3 with a mica or beryllium oxide washer, screwed to the chassis

children.note: Beryllium oxide isolators were common in power audio of the era; beryllium came from bertrandite and beryl ores and is toxic, which is why it was later replaced by bonded aluminium nitride and alumina.

The audio power amplifier is documented: it is the final electronic stage before the loudspeakers, its output may be a few watts for small consumer electronics devices such as clock radios, and many consumer electronics products including televisions have both a preamplifier and a power amplifier contained in a single chassis. That last sentence is direct backing for a television having its own amplifier. Not established: 2-5 W rms into 8 ohm from a 15-25 V DC rail as 1982 figures, the 5-20 W peak from a 115 V rail, the single 8-14 pin IC, the complementary NPN/PNP pair in a TO-3 or a plastic power package, and that the output stage ran class B or class AB. Whether the output was one IC or a discrete pair is a per-set design choice that no service manual was consulted for.

children.name: Volume potentiometer, carbon track
children.description: A rotary carbon track pot, typically 10 kohm or 100 kohm logarithmic (audio taper), spliced into the audio line. The track is a carbon film printed or sprayed on a phenolic or ceramic substrate; the wiper is a sprung brass or copper blade. This is the same technology as the volume control in a pocket radio, and the carbon comes from petroleum coke exactly as the CRT blackening does.

facts.label: Resistance
facts.value: 10-100 kohm, audio taper

children.note: Potentiometers are commonly the volume control on audio equipment, and carbon black is made by the incomplete combustion of coal tar, vegetable matter or petroleum products. Not established: the carbon film on a phenolic or ceramic substrate, the sprung brass or copper wiper, the 10-100 kohm audio taper and the 0.25-0.5 W rating.

children.name: Power supply: mains transformer and reservoir
children.description: Most 1982 sets were linear: a hot-chassis or a cold-chassis series/parallel mains transformer stepping 117 V down to about 110 V AC, a diode bridge rectifier, and a big electrolytic reservoir at 120 V feeding the line output. The main electrolytic was the largest, hottest component on the board and usually the first thing to dry out. A minority used a small switchmode supply for the logic rails with a flyback of its own.

facts.label: Reservoir
facts.value: 200-400 microfarad at 160 V, an aluminium can electrolytic

facts.label: Mains transformer
facts.value: E-I laminated silicon steel, 40-60 VA, potted or taped

children.note: A cold-chassis set had the mains referenced to the line output and the whole board was at mains potential; a hot-chassis set had an isolated secondary and a common return. Repairing a 1982 TV meant first determining which, which is why it was dangerous and why sets were sold with the chassis not user-serviceable. Not established: the 200-400 uF at 160 V reservoir value, the 115-120 V B+ at 0.4-0.6 A, and the 40-60 VA transformer rating for a 13 inch set.

children.name: Mains transformer, E-I silicon steel
children.description: A laminated core of thin silicon steel (about 0.35 mm) stamped into E and I shapes and stacked, with copper windings on bobbins, potted in epoxy or wrapped in tape and varnished. The laminations were needed because mains hum would otherwise magnetostrict the core; the 1982 design was exactly the design from the 1930s.

facts.label: Lamination
facts.value: 0.30-0.35 mm silicon steel, C5 or C21 grade

facts.label: Core frequency
facts.value: 60 Hz, so lamination is mandatory

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 40-60 VA for a 13 inch set

children.note: The silicon steel is a different alloy from the low-carbon steel of the shadow mask: it is deliberately alloyed with silicon to raise resistivity and suppress eddy currents, and it is a thin, carefully annealed strip. Both, though, came off a blast furnace. Electrical steel is made as cold-rolled strip under 2 mm thick, cut into laminations and stacked to form transformer cores, and grain-oriented grades run about 3% silicon. Not established: the 0.30-0.35 mm C5 or C21 lamination, the epoxy potting and taping, and the 40-60 VA rating for a 13 inch set.

children.name: Aluminium electrolytic reservoir, 200 microfarad 160 V
children.description: The reservoir is a wound aluminium foil anode with an oxide film formed on it, an aluminium cathode can, and a paper or synthetic-fibre separator soaked in electrolyte (an ammonium borate or an aluminium chloride solution in glycol). Formed at a few hundred volts, it hums and it leaks, and in a hot chassis it did the most to kill itself.

facts.label: Value
facts.value: 200-400 microfarad at 160 V

facts.label: Anode foil
facts.value: etched high-purity aluminium, 99.99%

facts.label: Electrolyte
facts.value: aluminium chloride or ammonium borate in ethylene glycol

children.note: The etched aluminium anode here is the same technology as the 1970s-80s consumer electrolytic capacitor and is documented in the mainboard's own power-supply branch. A 1982 TV reservoir was often one of the largest aluminium electrolytics made that year in a consumer product. A wet aluminium electrolytic is two aluminium foils separated by a paper spacer saturated with liquid or gel electrolyte, with the anode etched and formed; commercial parts run from 0.1 uF to 2.7 F at 4 V to 630 V, so a 200 uF 160 V reservoir is well inside the range. Not established: aluminium chloride or ammonium borate in ethylene glycol as the electrolyte, the 99.99% anode foil figure, and the claim that this was among the largest consumer electrolytics of 1982.

children.name: Mains rectifier bridge
children.description: Four silicon diodes in a moulded bridge package, rated at a few amps and 100-200 V. Cheap sets rectified with two diodes and a centre-tapped transformer instead. The bridge was usually on the chassis edge with the heatsink tab or in free air.
children.note: A diode bridge is four diodes converting AC to DC, and since about 1950 it has been a single four-terminal component made in various voltage and current ratings. Not established: the 1-4 A and 100-400 V rating, the moulded package, the chassis-edge mounting, and the two-diode centre-tapped alternative.

This node is the set's printed circuit board and its subassemblies, not a whole machine; the set itself stays computing. Not established: the 115-120 V B+ rail, the 4.5 MHz intercarrier audio and the 45.75 MHz picture carrier as values for a 1982 set.

children.name: Loudspeaker, 8 ohm, 3-4 inch
children.description: An 8 ohm speaker of about 3.5-4 inch diameter on a small set: a paper pulp cone, a pressed steel or plastic basket, a copper voice coil on a former, and a ferrite magnet. It was screwed to a baffle in the cabinet with the back magnet projecting into whatever space was left, which is why small speakers of the period often had a shallow magnet or a rear vent.

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 8 ohm nominal (4 ohm for parallel stereo)

facts.label: Size
facts.value: 3.5-4 inch diameter

facts.label: Frequency response
facts.value: about 200 Hz to 8-10 kHz in a small cabinet

children.name: Pressed steel basket
children.description: The cone is glued to a stamped steel basket that holds the magnet and the voice coil in register. It came off the same cold-reduced low-carbon sheet as the shadow mask and the chassis, with the same iron ore behind it.

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 150-250 g of steel in a 3.5 inch basket

facts.label: Joining
facts.value: spot welded or riveted to the magnet

children.note: The basket is stamped from the same cold-reduced low-carbon sheet as the shadow mask.

children.name: Copper voice coil on a former
children.description: Two layers of enamelled copper wire, about 40-60 turns, wound on a paper or aluminium former and centred in the magnet gap. It is a minute amount of copper, on the order of a gram, and it sits in a gap of under a millimetre.

facts.label: Turns
facts.value: 40-60, two layers

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 8 ohm DC resistance about 5-6 ohm

children.note: The voice coil is documented: a voice coil consisting of a former, collar and winding is the coil of wire attached to the apex of a loudspeaker cone, and it provides the motive force to the cone by the reaction of a magnetic field to the current passing through it. That is exactly this part. Not established: 40-60 turns in two layers, 8 ohm impedance with a 5-6 ohm DC resistance, on the order of a gram of copper, and the sub-millimetre gap. An 8 ohm two-layer winding of tens of turns on a small paper or aluminium former is the ordinary construction of a small television speaker, so the shape of the figures is right; the numbers themselves are a reconstruction.

The part of a small loudspeaker that decides what industry it belongs to is the sintered ferrite ring and the winding in its gap. Hard ferrites are used to make permanent magnets for loudspeakers, and the voice coil moves axially in a cylindrical gap in a permanent magnet's field. Not established: 8 ohm, 3.5-4 inch, 2-5 W, and the 200 Hz to 8-10 kHz response in a small cabinet.

children.name: Cabinet and front bezel
children.description: The outside of the set: a moulded plastics shell wrapped around the chassis and the tube, with a wood-grain print or a real veneer. A 1982 13 inch set was typically an injection-moulded ABS or ABS/polycarbonate cabinet, textured, with the front bezel carrying the speaker grille, the control knobs and the brand badge. Larger and older-style sets had a wood-veneered or wood-framed cabinet; the very cheapest had a printed paper laminate over a steel or plastic shell.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ABS, or ABS/polycarbonate blend, textured leatherette

facts.label: Moulding
facts.value: injection moulded at 220-260 degrees C, 40-70 seconds cycle

facts.label: Front
facts.value: ABS bezel with a printed or moulded speaker grille

children.note: Wood-plastic (particle board faced with a melamine or polyester woodgrain laminate) was used on the console-style and portable sets of the era; the true ABS shell took over on the small sets. Both the woodgrain-print cabinet and the real veneer cabinet are worth covering, and both appear here. Not established: ABS or ABS/polycarbonate as the 1982 cabinet material, the 220-260 C and 40-70 s cycle, and the 13 inch size. The Reynosa, Taipei and Japan production attributions are not established either.

children.name: Wood veneer or woodgrain laminate
children.description: A console or a large set of the early 1980s was often a real cabinet: a wood frame veneered with walnut, mahogany or teak, sometimes over particle board. The cheaper route was a printed polyester or melamine laminate, several sheets laminated and printed with a photographic woodgrain. A 13 inch portable used moulded ABS with the grain embossed into the mould texture and painted.

facts.label: Veneer
facts.value: 0.6 mm sliced or rotary cut, about 4-8 leaves per log

facts.label: Particle board
facts.value: wood chips pressed at about 8-10 MPa with a urea or phenol binder

facts.label: Laminate
facts.value: melamine-impregnated paper or a polyester film printed with a woodgrain

children.note: Again the one renewable leaf: a veneer cabinet is wood and board, not a polymer. A tree, cut and sliced. Check the type on a console set of the period and it is very often plastic, but this node is the case where it was not.

children.name: Case screws and brackets
children.description: The chassis was fastened into the cabinet with self-tapping screws into plastic bosses, and the back was held with a handful of machine screws into zinc-plated or black-oxide steel. The brackets that carried the tube and the board were zinc-plated sheet steel.

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: zinc electroplate, or a mechanical zinc flake coating

children.note: Zinc plating is the zinc electroplating industry, and zinc came from the same sphalerite chain as the CRT phosphor. Another convergence.

children.name: Brand badge and control knobs
children.description: The logo badge was an embossed or plated plastic medallion, and the knobs were moulded ABS or phenolic on a zinc or aluminium die-cast core with a moulded pointer. On a cheap set the badge was printed; on a good one it was a plated plastic insert.
inputs: zinc alloy or aluminium die casting

facts.label: Knob core
facts.value: zinc alloy die-cast, an early use of high-pressure die casting for a consumer knob

children.note: No source was found for any of this. A moulded or plated badge and moulded knobs on the front panel are certainly present on a 1982 set, and a metal core inside a knob to carry the moulding and the torque is ordinary practice. Not established: that the knob core was a zinc alloy or aluminium die casting and that this counted as an early high-pressure die casting use for a consumer knob, the embossed or plated plastic medallion badge, chrome or nickel plating, the moulded pointer, and the claim that cheap sets had a printed badge and good ones a plated insert. Neither the alloy nor the badge construction can be given for a particular set, and the wording of the claim about which end of the market did what is a generalisation about badged sets rather than a documented survey.

children.name: Front controls: pots, switches, dial
children.description: Brightness, contrast, colour, tint, volume and the channel selector, plus a fine-tuning and a V-hold behind the cabinet. The pots are carbon track or cermet; the switches are an AC line switch and often a rotary band switch or push-buttons for the a/v functions.

facts.label: Brightness and colour
facts.value: usually 5 kohm or 10 kohm linear

facts.label: Volume
facts.value: 10 kohm or 100 kohm audio taper

facts.label: Switch
facts.value: rotary AC mains switch on the volume pot shaft on many sets

children.name: AC line switch and interlock
children.description: A rotary or push-pull mains switch on the front panel, often interlocked so that a set with a back cover off could not be switched on (the 'interlock' on a portable). The switch contacts were silver-plated brass, and the whole switch was a snap-action mechanism in a phenolic body.

facts.label: Contacts
facts.value: silver-plated brass, rated at a few amps at 250 V

facts.label: Interlock
facts.value: a cover switch so a serviceable set could not be energised with the back open

children.note: No source was found for the construction. A mains on-off switch with a positive gap, and a cover interlock that prevents a partially disassembled set being energised, are both real and well-known features of sets of the period. Not established: silver-plated brass contacts as the universal contact material, a rating of a few amps at 250 V, the phenolic body with a snap-action mechanism, and the specific claim that the switch was rotary or push-pull on the front panel. A mains switch integrated with the volume control was also common, so the position of this switch is not settled either.

children.name: VHF dial and channel drum
children.description: The channel numbers were on a printed drum or card behind a window, or on a flat dial plate, driven by the cord from the knob. The UHF channels 14-83 needed a drum or a fan-shaped card because there were 70 of them, which is why UHF dials of the period were a distinctive piece of mechanical design.

facts.label: UHF
facts.value: 70 channels, so a drum or a rotating card rather than a straight scale

children.note: No source was found for the mechanism. The problem described is a real one: a large number of channel numbers will not fit on a straight scale, so a drum, a fan-shaped card or a rotating disc is the ordinary solution and a cord and pulley drive from the knob is the ordinary way of turning it. Not established: that a printed card or drum sat behind a window, that the UHF channels were the reason for the drum specifically, the number of channels on the card, nylon gears, and the dial cord. The historical detail that channel numbers moved onto a disc and later onto a remote-control entry system is a design narrative, not a documented statement.
Not established: 5 kohm or 10 kohm linear pots for brightness and colour, 10 kohm or 100 kohm audio taper for volume, and the rotary mains switch on the volume pot shaft.

children.name: Aerial input and antenna lead
children.description: The 75 ohm coaxial aerial socket at the back, the twin-lead alternative for indoor aerials, and the telescopic whip on a portable. The C64 was plugged into that socket, in parallel with whatever aerial the set had. The socket was either a threaded F-type, or a cheaper bayonet or push-on type in Europe.

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm coaxial (or 300 ohm balanced twin-lead)

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: F-type threaded, or a bayonet in the UK

facts.label: Bandwidth
facts.value: to 890 MHz for UHF

children.name: F-type coaxial connector
children.description: A threaded, quarter-turn connector for 75 ohm coax, usually brass with a nickel or cadmium plate and a dielectric insert of PTFE or polyethylene. Brass is copper-zinc, so this little part pulls from both the copper and the zinc industry; the zinc can also be the zinc plated steel shell.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: brass (60% Cu, 40% Zn) with a nickel or cadmium plate

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: PTFE or polyethylene insert

facts.label: Center contact
facts.value: brass or copper with a silver or nickel plating

children.note: The F connector is documented as the common coaxial television aerial connector, normally used with RG-6/U or RG-59/U cable, and coaxial replaced twin-lead. That is the function and the standard. Not established: the 60% Cu / 40% Zn brass body (an F connector body is commonly nickel-plated brass, but the exact alloy is not fixed by the standard), the nickel or cadmium plate, the PTFE or polyethylene dielectric insert, the silver or nickel plated centre contact, the 75 ohm characteristic impedance as a specification of the connector rather than of the cable, and the Taiwan and United States works. Note that the centre contact and the shell are separate plated parts and need not use the same finish; this node gives both without saying which is which.

children.name: Telescopic whip antenna
children.description: On a portable set, a telescopic whip: a chrome-plated steel rod in a plastic base, with a ball joint for the angle. It was a whip antenna for VHF, and on UHF-only portables it was a loop inside the cabinet.

facts.label: Rod
facts.value: chrome-plated carbon or stainless steel, 3-6 sections

children.note: No source was found for the construction. A telescopic whip on a portable set is a real and ordinary part, and a sectional rod sliding in a moulded base with a swivel is the standard way one is built. Not established: that the rod was carbon or stainless steel rather than solid brass or a steel tube with a plastic taper, the chrome plating being on the rod rather than a separate decorative sleeve, three to six sections, the ABS base, the ball joint, and the claim that UHF-only portables used an internal loop. The 3-6 mm diameter of a telescopic whip section is also unstated and unverified; the collapsed length is what constrained the diameter, and no drawing was consulted.

The F connector is the common coaxial television aerial connector, normally used with RG-6/U or RG-59/U cable, and coaxial replaced twin-lead. Not established: 300 ohm balanced twin-lead as the alternative, the bayonet type in the UK, and the 890 MHz UHF bandwidth.

children.name: Mains lead, suppression filter and fuse
children.description: A 1982 set had a two or three core mains lead, an entrapment and bypass capacitor for radio interference, and one or two fuses. The mains filter is the reason a television did not buzz on an AM radio, and the reason the plastic of a 1980s set smelled faintly of phenolic. The fuse was a small glass or ceramic cartridge with a wire or a metal link.

facts.label: Mains
facts.value: 117 V 60 Hz (US) or 240 V 50 Hz (EU)

facts.label: Bypass capacitor
facts.value: 0.01-0.05 microfarad at about 400-600 V DC, X-rated

facts.label: Entrapment
facts.value: a common-mode choke of about 1-2 mH or a strap of ferrite around the line

children.name: Mains cord, PVC jacket over stranded copper
children.description: A flexible cord of 16 or 18 AWG stranded copper inside a PVC or rubber jacket, moulded on to the plug and to the set's inlet. The set's inlet on a 1982 television was not an IEC C13 appliance coupler (that became common on computers and later sets); most were a hard-wired rubber or vinyl cord straight into the chassis, with a moulded two-pin or three-pin plug at the wall end. A detachable cord on a set was unusual until the mid 1980s.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 16 or 18 AWG stranded, flexible, rated 250 V

facts.label: Jacket
facts.value: PVC or a thermoset rubber, 2-3 core

facts.label: Plug
facts.value: moulded-on two-pin (US, with the grounded case pin) or three-pin

children.note: An IEC-ish inlet belongs to the C64's own power supply unit, not to the television. What belongs to the television is the hard-wired cord and the moulded plug, which are covered here.

children.name: Mains suppression: X capacitor and common-mode choke
children.description: A high-voltage capacitor across line and neutral (the X capacitor) plus a ferrite-beaded choke in series, to keep the set's switching noise out of the radio. In a 1982 set this was often a paper or film capacitor at 0.01 microfarad rated for mains transients; the modern purple or orange epoxy-drop X capacitor of the 1990s had not appeared, though a metallised film in a plastic case was used. The choke was a few turns on a ferrite or powdered-iron core.

facts.label: X capacitor
facts.value: 0.01-0.05 microfarad, mains-transient rated

facts.label: Choke
facts.value: 1-2 mH common mode, or a ferrite strap

children.name: Metallised polypropylene mains capacitor
children.description: A polypropylene or polystyrene film, vacuum-metallised with a thin aluminium layer on both faces, wound and potted in epoxy. It was the capacitor of choice across the line because a self-healing metallisation would recover from a mains transient rather than failing short. Polystyrene was also used for its stability and low microphonics.

facts.label: Voltage
facts.value: 400-630 V DC working for a mains suppression position

facts.label: Self-healing
facts.value: a transient punctures the oxide and evaporises the metal locally

children.note: Metallized film is documented as polymer plastic film coated with a thin layer of metal, usually aluminium, used for specialty applications including electronics. That establishes the construction. Not established: the 400-630 V DC working rating as a 1982 mains suppression rating, the self-healing mechanism as described (a fault punctures the oxide and vaporises the metallisation locally, which is the standard account, but no source was consulted for it here), polystyrene as a dielectric in this position, and epoxy potting. A film capacitor across the line has to be a safety-rated part, and a plain metallised film wrapped in epoxy is a different part from a certified X-rated one; which of the two a 1982 set carried is not established.

No source was found. The need is documented by the existence of the parts: a capacitor across line and neutral and a series choke or ferrite bead in a mains lead are ordinary EMI-suppression components, and they are here for emissions and for immunity rather than for filtering the supply itself. Not established: that the device was called an X capacitor in 1982 - the IEC safety capacitor classes X1, X2 and Y were introduced in the 1980s and the class name postdates many of the sets that already shipped the part - the 0.01-0.05 microfarad value, the 1-2 mH common-mode choke, and the claim that a drop-in epoxy X capacitor of the 1990s had not appeared. What is well documented is the end of the chain: modern mains filters are built from exactly these two elements.

children.name: Mains fuse
children.description: A 3-4 amp buss fuse in the mains lead holder on sets with a detachable cord, or an internal fuse on the line. The fuse element was a low-melting alloy or a silver wire in a glass cartridge.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 3-4 A, 250 V, time delay on larger sets

children.note: The mains fuse is a European (IEC) style addition that many US sets of the period lacked, having a non-rewirable fuse only in the more expensive models.

This is the set's power entry: a cord, a suppression network and a fuse. Not established: the X-rated 0.01-0.05 uF bypass capacitor at 400-600 V, the 1-2 mH common-mode choke or ferrite strap, and the phenolic smell. 117 V 60 Hz and 240 V 50 Hz are regional mains rather than a figure for any one set.

children.name: Datasette and cassette
children.description: A C64 with no drive could not save. Commodore's answer was a 1530 or 1541 disk-shaped drive that took ordinary compact cassettes and wrote them with a magnetic head at 9,600 baud, plus a spool of tape that was mostly polyester film and mostly iron oxide. Saving a 1541 program to tape was a two minute operation of real-time winding, and the alignment problems of a 1541 were a running joke precisely because a cassette had no feedback.

facts.label: Drive
facts.value: 1530 (Series I, 4,800 baud) or 1541 (Series II, 9,600 baud)

facts.label: Tape
facts.value: standard compact cassette, C-60 or C-90, 1/8 inch wide

facts.label: Tape speed
facts.value: 4.76 cm/s (1 7/8 inches per second)

facts.label: Power
facts.value: 5 V and about 12 V DC, both from the C64's own supply via the cassette port

children.note: The 1541 had no mains supply of its own. It drew 5 V (through a fuse and reverse-polarity diode) and about 12 V from pins 4-7 of the C64's cassette port. The 1530 datasette was the same idea in a different box, with the tape slot on top and a position sensor; the 1541 is the one people remember because it had no position sensor at all.

children.name: The 1541 disk drive
children.description: A disk-shaped grey box with a slot on top, containing a stepper motor, a capstan flywheel, a read/write head on a load arm, and a small circuit board with a 6502 CPU, a 6522 interface chip and a mask-programmed logic array. It reads and writes the same standard compact cassette as a music cassette deck, which is why Commodore's error messages included CLOAD and why a music cassette recorder could in principle play a C64 tape.

facts.label: Format
facts.value: GCR (group code recording) at 4,800 or 9,600 baud

facts.label: Head gap
facts.value: about 1 micrometre

facts.label: Capacity
facts.value: about 170 KB per side as used by the 1541

facts.label: Alignment
facts.value: no position sensor; the drive counts steps

children.name: 6502 CPU, 6522 PIA and M50174 PLA
children.description: The 1541's electronics are almost identical in content to the C64's, which is not a coincidence: Commodore reused its own chips. A 6502 runs the operating system and the serial protocol; a 6522 versatile interface adapter talks to the tape, drives the stepper and reads the serial bus to the C64; and a mask-programmed logic array, the M50174, handles the address decode and the stepper phase sequencing so the CPU does not have to bit-bang them.

facts.label: CPU
facts.value: MOS 6502, clocked at about 1 MHz from the bus

facts.label: PIA
facts.value: 6522, 40-pin DIP, two 8-bit ports with handshaking and timers

facts.label: PLA
facts.value: M50174, a custom mask-programmed logic array

facts.label: Process
facts.value: 6502 on NMOS at about 4-5 microns; the PLA on a mask-programmed CMOS or bipolar process

places: Philadelphia (MOS Technology lineage), then Japan, Taiwan and Hong Kong for the volume runs
children.note: The 1541's clock is a point of real uncertainty. It does not run a free oscillator; it takes a timebase from the cassette-port timing supplied by the C64's VIC-II, and the CPU is clocked at about 1 MHz derived from that. The exact divider chain is a reverse-engineering result, not a design intent, so no figure more precise than about 1 MHz is established. The M50174's process technology is also uncertain; it may have been bipolar rather than CMOS.

children.name: The silicon this logic is made from
children.description: The 6502, the 6522 and the PLA were all made on 1980-era processes: a 3-5 micron NMOS or bipolar line, or a custom bipolar array. The wafer was the same trichlorosilane-to-polysilicon-to-epitaxy chain already traced under the television's video IC, and the die was diced, wire-bonded and epoxy-moulded.

facts.label: Line
