facts.value: 3-5 micron NMOS for the 6502, 5 micron NMOS for the 6522

facts.label: Mould compound
facts.value: phenolic or epoxy with silica filler, transfer or compression moulded

children.note: The integrated circuit is documented as printed as a unit by photolithography onto a thin flat piece of semiconductor material, most commonly silicon, which is the mechanism this node describes for the drive logic. Not established: that a 1982 disk drive carried a 6502, a 6522 and a mask-programmed array on the same processes as each other (a CMOS or bipolar logic array is a different process from an NMOS CPU), the 3-5 micron and 5 micron line figures as drive silicon, phenolic mould compound, and the Hong Kong and Taiwan works. Those line figures belong to the machine processor and are documented there; a disk drive is a different buyer of the same industry. Aluminium interconnect over polysilicon is also a later generation than the early 1980s, so it should not be read as a 1982 statement.

children.name: Hybrid stepping motor
children.description: A hybrid stepping motor: a permanent-magnet rotor with fine teeth running between two toothed stator poles, with coils on the poles. Two phases driven in sequence step the rotor a fraction of a degree at a time. This is how the 1541 knew where the tape was, and the motor's own inertia is why a 1541 could not skip forward as fast as it could seek.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: 2-phase hybrid, permanent-magnet rotor

facts.label: Step angle
facts.value: of the order of 2.5-5 degrees, with microstepping in the drive logic

facts.label: Windings
facts.value: two bifilar or four independent coils, tens of ohms each

facts.label: Rotor
facts.value: sintered ferrite or Alnico permanent magnet with 24-50 fine teeth

facts.label: Torque
facts.value: about 0.1-0.5 newton-metres, enough to turn the capstan and the head load cam against the tape

children.note: The 1541's motor step angle and rotor construction are not established; the qualitative description (two-phase hybrid PM motor driving the capstan through a worm reduction, with the same rotation also positioning the head load) is solid, the numbers are not. Some sources describe the 1541 motor as a 2.5-degree step with 40 steps per revolution; others suggest a coarser angle with half-stepping. Treat the numbers as indicative.

children.name: Toothed stator laminations of silicon steel
children.description: The stator is a stack of thin silicon steel laminations with fine teeth, each pole carrying a bobbin of magnet wire. The laminations are punched from the same 0.35 mm silicon steel as the television's mains transformer, but the teeth are punched to a pitch of well under a millimetre, which is the reason a hybrid stepper has far more rotor teeth than its stator poles.

facts.label: Lamination
facts.value: 0.35-0.5 mm silicon steel, eddy-current-grade

facts.label: Tooth pitch
facts.value: about 0.5-1 mm, fine compared with a mains transformer

facts.label: Windings
facts.value: 30-50 turns of 0.2-0.3 mm enamelled wire per pole

children.note: A stepper motor is documented as a brushless DC electric motor that rotates in a series of small and discrete angular steps and can be set to any given step position without needing a position sensor for feedback; switched-reluctance motors are described as very large stepping motors with a reduced pole count. The 1541 documentation confirms that the drive moved its head with a stepper motor, driven from the 6522 port B: PB 1 is STP 0, step motor for head movement. Not established: the 0.35-0.5 mm silicon steel lamination thickness, the sub-millimetre tooth pitch, 30-50 turns of 0.2-0.3 mm enamelled wire per pole, and that the laminations were the same grade as a television mains transformer used. A hybrid stepper rotor does carry many more teeth than the stator has poles, so the argument about the tooth pitch is sound; the numbers are not sourced.

children.name: End bells, bushings and the mounting bracket
children.description: The motor is held between two stamped steel end bells with bronze or sintered bronze bushings for the shafts (or plastic bushings on a cheap drive), and mounted on a steel bracket riveted or screwed into the deck. The whole assembly sat on a die-cast or folded steel chassis plate.

facts.label: Bushing
facts.value: sintered bronze or oil-impregnated sintered iron, or a PTFE-impregnated plastic sleeve

children.note: The 1541's motor bearings were a well-known source of squeal and alignment trouble; whether they were bronze or sintered iron is not established. The end bells and bushings are stamped steel and sintered bronze, and the part belongs to the motor.

children.name: Tape transport: capstan, pinch roller, worm reduction
children.description: The cassette slid in and the tape was pressed against a capstan on the drive by a rubber pinch roller, at 4.76 cm/s. The capstan was on a flywheel turned by the stepper motor through a worm reduction, which also let the motor's back-driving put the capstan in the right phase. The same motor rotation drove a cam that loaded the head against the tape. There was no tachometer, no position sensor and no closed loop: the drive simply counted steps and hoped.

facts.label: Capstan
facts.value: 2.0-2.5 mm diameter hardened steel pin, 4.76 cm/s at the surface

facts.label: Flywheel
facts.value: a die-cast aluminium or moulded plastic flywheel on the capstan shaft

facts.label: Worm reduction
facts.value: a single or multi-start worm on the motor shaft meshing a nylon or brass worm wheel on the capstan shaft

facts.label: Pinch roller
facts.value: a 6-8 mm rubber roller on a spring-loaded arm, driven off the motor by a friction wheel or a belt

facts.label: Head load
facts.value: a cam and spring arm that pressed the head into the cassette window; some drives kept it permanently in contact

children.note: The 1541 kept the head in contact with the tape at all times rather than loading it, which is part of why it was so noisy and why a 1541 could hear your programme as well as read it. The exact worm ratio is not established, and whether the head was loadable is not either; several 1541 variants kept the head permanently engaged.

children.name: Pinch roller and rubber
children.description: A small roller of black nitrile or butyl rubber on a moulded plastic or nylon hub, on a bent spring steel arm. The rubber had to grip the capstan and the tape without slipping and without depositing rubber onto the tape, and a dried-out pinch roller was the single most common cause of a 1541 failing to read a tape it had just written.

facts.label: Rubber
facts.value: nitrile (butadiene-acrylonitrile) or butyl, 60-80 Shore A

facts.label: Diameter
facts.value: 6-8 mm, the roller pressing the tape against the capstan

children.note: Nitrile rubber comes from butadiene and acrylonitrile, the same two monomers as the ABS of a television cabinet, both from crude oil. Rubber and plastics in 1982 shared the same petrochemical feedstock. Only the spring-steel arm is currently linked (to music wire); the rubber has no nitrile/butyl substance node and the hub material is unattested as nylon versus acetal, so neither is forced onto an edge.

children.name: Worm and worm-wheel reduction
children.description: The stepper's rotation was reduced by a worm on the motor shaft running in a nylon or brass wheel on the capstan shaft. A worm gear is quiet and gives a high ratio in a small space and is self-locking, which is exactly what is wanted: when the power was off the capstan could not back-drive. The wheel was usually a moulded nylon or acetal wheel with a brass insert.

facts.label: Worm
facts.value: hardened steel, single or multi-start, 5-10 mm diameter

facts.label: Wheel
facts.value: nylon or acetal, or a brass wheel, 15-30 mm diameter

children.note: A worm gear is naturally self-locking, which is what stopped a 1541's capstan spinning backwards when the C64 was switched off.

children.name: Capstan, hardened steel pin
children.description: Hardened steel pin, 2.0-2.5 mm diameter, ground finish; the tape wraps it against the pinch roller and its surface speed (4.76 cm/s) defines tape speed. Takes the wear; self-locking worm drive prevents back-driving when unpowered.

children.name: Read/write head, gap about 1 micrometre
children.description: A miniature magnetic recording head, essentially the same object as the one in a cassette deck but smaller and more carefully shielded. A ferrite or permalloy core with a laser-cut gap of about a micrometre, a figure-eight winding of lacquered copper to cancel hum from the drive's own motor, a mumetal shield can around the front, and a printed circuit board carrying the preamplifier right at the head to keep the signal short.

facts.label: Gap
facts.value: about 1 micrometre (0.5-2 micrometres depending on head)

facts.label: Core
facts.value: ferrite or permalloy (mumetal) with a mu-metal shield

facts.label: Winding
facts.value: about 500-1500 turns of 40 AWG (0.1 mm) enamelled copper

facts.label: Hum cancelling
facts.value: figure-eight winding so the drive motor's stray field cancels

facts.label: Bias
facts.value: short-wavelength (standard, about 120 ns) bias for the C64 format

facts.label: Resolution
facts.value: on a standard-bias cassette the short-wavelength limit is a few thousand transitions per inch

children.note: The gap figure of about 1 micrometre is the standard audio-cassette head gap. The bias figure is the important one for the C64: the 1541 wrote standard-bias (about 120 ns, short-wavelength) tape, which is why a C-90 or C-120 high-bias (1200 ns, long-wavelength) tape gave poor results on a 1541 and why Commodore recommended standard C-60 and C-90 tapes. The flux interval the C64 used was roughly 200-310 microseconds, about 3.2-4.8 kHz, which is 1700-2600 flux transitions per inch at 4.76 cm/s against a standard-bias cassette limit of about 3200 per inch, which is firmly in the short-wavelength region and near the limit of what a standard-bias tape could resolve; that is the physical reason a 1541 was fussy about tape formulation.

children.name: The 1541 circuit board
children.description: A single FR-4 board with the CPU, the PIA, the PLA, a handful of logic gates, the head preamplifier, the stepper driver transistors, and the power regulators. It was a through-hole board in 1982, socketed for the CPU and the PIA so they could be replaced, and hand- or wave-soldered.

facts.label: Sockets
facts.value: 40-pin DIP sockets for the 6502 and the 6522

facts.label: Solder
facts.value: 60/40 tin-lead on tin-plated through-holes

facts.label: Stepper drive
facts.value: discrete transistors, or a small IC, driving two phases

facts.label: Laminate
facts.value: 1.6 mm single-sided FR-4, 35 micron copper foil, epoxy mask, 60/40 tin-lead

children.note: The FR-4 laminate, copper foil, solder mask and tin-lead solder are the same chain as the television's PCB, documented under peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb, and they are ingredients of this board rather than parts of it. Not established: the single-sided 1.6 mm FR-4 with 35 micron copper foil, the 40-pin DIP sockets for the 6502 and 6522, and the discrete-versus-IC stepper drive. The 6502 CPU, the 6522 interface chip and the mask-programmed logic array are documented under this node's own children.

children.name: Power supply: 5 V and 12 V from the C64
children.description: The 1541 has no mains input. It gets 5 V and about 12 V DC from the C64 through the six-pin cassette port, and regulates them locally: the 12 V feeds the motor and the head bias, the 5 V feeds the logic, and a linear regulator or a discrete dropper makes the 5 V from a higher rail on some models. There was a fuse and a reverse-polarity protection diode because the port was known to be a point of user error.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: 5 V logic and 9-12 V motor/bias, via the 6-pin cassette connector

facts.label: Current
facts.value: about 0.4-0.7 A drawn while a tape moves

facts.label: Regulation
facts.value: linear, or a simple zener/transistor dropper

children.note: The exact regulator topology of a 1541 varies by revision, and no part can be named with confidence. What is certain and important is that the drive was powered entirely from the computer, which is why a 1541 and its C64 shared one power supply and one mains lead.

children.name: The regulator and its electrolytics
children.description: The 1541 regulated the 9-12 V rail down to 5 V with a small linear regulator or a discrete zener-transmitter, and used a handful of aluminium electrolytics to ripple-filter it. Both are the same parts as the television reservoir: etched four-nines aluminium foil in a wound foil anode, with a fibre separator and a chloride or borate electrolyte.
inputs: aluminium chloride or ammonium borate electrolyte

facts.label: Values
facts.value: about 10-470 microfarad at 10-25 V on a 1541

facts.label: Ripple
facts.value: a few tens of millivolts at the logic rail

children.note: An aluminium electrolytic is documented as two aluminium foils separated by a paper spacer saturated with liquid or gel electrolyte, with the anode etched and formed, with commercial parts from 0.1 uF to 2.7 F at 4 V to 630 V - so a few hundred microfarad at a low voltage is comfortably inside the range and the reservoir at the other end of the same branch is a real comparator. Not established: that the drive regulated with a small linear regulator or a discrete zener-transistor as described, the 10-470 microfarad values, the tens of millivolts of ripple at the logic rail, and the Hong Kong and Taiwan works. The etched-foil construction is the technology; which capacitor values a given drive populated is a schematic detail. Two regulators in series would be a design smell, and whether this was one device or two is exactly what is not established here.

children.name: The 1541 plastic case
children.description: A grey ABS clamshell, disc-shaped, about 40 cm across and 9 cm deep, moulded in two halves with the lid carrying the Commodore logo badge and the slot for the cassette. The material is the same ABS as a television cabinet, from the same styrene-butadiene-acrylonitrile chemistry.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: about 400 mm across, 90 mm deep

facts.label: Colour
facts.value: grey, the colour Commodore specified for the drive and for the C64's case-adjacent parts

facts.label: Moulding
facts.value: two-shot clamshell, 230-260 degrees C ABS

children.note: The case is moulded from the same ABS grade as a television cabinet, and it reaches the monomers through the styrene-butadiene-acrylonitrile petrochemical chain rather than through the cabinet. Not established: the two-shot clamshell construction, the about 400 mm by 90 mm dimensions, the 230-260 C ABS moulding, and the claim that the drive's ABS was the same grade as a television cabinet's.

children.name: Activity LED
children.description: A small red LED on the front of the drive, lit while the motor was running or the head was active. It was a gallium arsenide or gallium phosphide die in a 2.5 mm epoxy lens, running at about 2-10 mA from the 5 V rail through a resistor. The LED itself was 1980s technology; the indicator lamps on earlier drives had been incandescent bulbs or neon.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: GaAs or GaP, with a GaAsP window for red

facts.label: Forward drop
facts.value: about 1.7-2.2 V, current 2-10 mA

facts.label: Epoxy lens
facts.value: 2.5 mm or 3 mm, with the die mounted in a reflector cup

children.note: Efficient diode emission from GaAs was patented in 1962 and commercial LEDs only became practical once they cost under five cents in the 1970s. Not established: GaAs or GaP die with a GaAsP window for red, the 1.7-2.2 V forward drop, the 2-10 mA running current, and the 2.5 mm epoxy lens with a reflector cup.

children.name: The nine-pin serial link to the C64
children.description: The 1541 connected to the C64 by a nine-pin high-density D-subminiature cable carrying the serial bus, which is how the drive knew there was a computer and the computer knew there was a drive.

children.note: The drive is an intelligent peripheral with its own processor and control system, connected to the C64 or VIC-20 over the serial bus at device number 4-15. Not established: the GCR 4,800 or 9,600 baud rate, the about 1 micrometre head gap, the 170 KB per side as the 1541 used it, and the absence of a position sensor.

children.name: The cassette tape itself
children.description: A compact cassette is a 3.81 mm wide strip of polyester film 12 microns thick, coated on one side with about one to two microns of acicular iron oxide pigment in a binder, and wound onto hubs inside a plastic shell. The C64 wrote 9,600 baud onto it, which at 4.76 cm/s works out to a flux transition every 200 to 300 microseconds, near the limit of what a standard-bias cassette could resolve. Almost everything in it is either crude oil or iron ore.

facts.label: Tape width
facts.value: 3.81 mm (1/8 inch)

facts.label: Base film
facts.value: polyester (PET), 9-12 microns

facts.label: Coating
facts.value: about 1-2 microns of gamma-Fe2O3 (or CrO2 for Type II)

facts.label: Areal density
facts.value: roughly 4-9 g/m2 of magnetite, so a whole 90 m C-60 carries only 1-3 g of iron oxide

facts.label: Coercivity
facts.value: about 25-30 kA/m standard bias; 45-55 kA/m for CrO2

facts.label: Remanence
facts.value: about 0.25-0.3 T

facts.label: C60 length
facts.value: 90 m total, 45 m per side at 4.76 cm/s

facts.label: Oxide
facts.value: iron(III) oxide or, for Type II, chromium dioxide

children.note: A C64 could use a standard C-60, a C-90, and in principle any compact cassette. Commodore recommended particular brands because the format was sensitive to tape formulation: a high-bias C-120 tape was on the wrong bias wavelength for the 1541, and a Type II chrome tape had a different coercivity and a different noise floor.

children.name: Cassette shell and hubs
children.description: The compact cassette case: two thin polystyrene or ABS shells, each with a hub, so that the tape is enclosed in a rigid 100 x 64 x 12 mm box with five windows on one edge for the head, capstan and the pressure pad, two hub windows, and the write-protect notches. The hubs were glass-filled nylon or moulded ABS with the six drive slots, running on the two hub spindles.

facts.label: Shell
facts.value: about 100 x 64 x 12 mm, injection moulded polystyrene or ABS

facts.label: Hub
facts.value: glass-filled nylon or ABS, six drive slots, bore about 22 mm

facts.label: Window layout
facts.value: two capstan holes, a head window (erase and R/P), five pressure-pad windows (C1-C5), two hub windows

facts.label: Write protect
facts.value: recesses in the shell; a plug in two of them blocks the sense switch

facts.label: Screws
facts.value: five small screws joining the two shells, with the tape trapped between them

children.note: The five pressure-pad windows are the IEC C-1 to C-5 positions. The felt pad inside the shell, pressed against the tape by the capstan bulge, biases the tape against one of the shell's internal ribs so that, depending on how the shell is placed in the deck, the tape passes over the erase head, between the erase and R/P heads, over the R/P head, or not in contact with either. That is why a cassette's orientation and which end is which mattered, and why a mis-loaded tape would write nothing. The mechanism is certain; the precise numbering of which position does what is less certain. Not established: the IEC C-1 to C-5 pressure-pad window numbering and which position lands on which head - the node's own note already concedes this - the about 22 mm hub bore, and glass-filled nylon as the hub material, since this file's hub node gives nylon 66. The five-screw two-shell construction and the 100 x 64 x 12 mm envelope are the standard part.

children.name: Hub, glass-filled nylon
children.description: The reel hub runs on the shell's spindle and drives the tape through a wind process. It had to be dimensionally stable and dimensionally tight so the tape wound at a given radius came off at the right tension. It was glass-filled nylon or ABS, with the six drive slots on the inside face for the winding spindle.

facts.label: Bore
facts.value: an inner bore of order 20 mm that slips over the cassette moulded spindle; the exact IEC figure is not certain here

facts.label: Drive slots
facts.value: six internal slots, the standard cassette hub pattern

children.note: The six-slot hub pattern and the general hub geometry are certain; the bore diameter is not verified against the IEC dimension, so it is stated loosely. The hub is moulded from nylon 66, chem.polyamide.nylon-66.

children.name: Pressure pad and felt
children.description: A small pad of felt or synthetic non-woven on a stainless steel leaf spring, mounted in a plastic carrier inside the shell behind the head window. Its job was to press the tape gently against the head so the head could read and write reliably, and to press the tape against the shell's ribs to select the C-1 to C-5 path. The felt was the one consumable part of a cassette; it shed debris into the head gap and a worn pad was a classic cause of a 1541 failing.

facts.label: Felt
facts.value: about 0.5-1 mm of wool felt or a bonded polyester fibre

facts.label: Force
facts.value: a few tenths of a newton, enough for good contact without jamming the tape

children.note: Felt pads are wool, a textile, and polyester non-wovens were the synthetic alternative. Either way this is not a mined or drilled raw material but a processed fibre.

children.name: The connectors: aerial socket, serial link, user port, cassette port
children.description: Three connectors that made a C64 usable rather than just powered: the aerial socket the RF modulator hijacked, the nine-pin link to the 1541, and the cartridge-edge expansion connector on the back that opened the machine up - documented as a 44-pin card edge, not a 34-conductor ribbon.

children.name: The aerial socket, hijacked
children.description: The 75 ohm coaxial socket on the back of the television. The C64's modulator lead was a short 75 ohm coax with an F-type plug that went into it in parallel with the set's aerial. Because the modulator was a weak source, the lead had to be a good 75 ohm match and the set's aerial input had to be isolated or the local signal would back-feed.

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm

facts.label: Lead
facts.value: about 1.5 m of RG-59, supplied with the C64

children.note: The modulator's coax lead and the set's own aerial lead are both ingredients of this socket rather than parts of it. An RF cable was a listed C64 accessory (C 326189-01), and the RF modulator mixed sync/luminance, colour and audio to generate a TV composite signal on pin 5. Not established for the supplied lead: 75 ohm, RG-59 and the about 1.5 m length - the F connector is normally used with RG-6/U or RG-59/U.

children.name: Nine-pin serial link to the drive
children.description: The 1541 was not daisy-chained through the cassette port; it plugged into the C64's second serial port through a nine-pin high-density D-subminiature cable. That separate port is how the computer knew a disk drive was present at all: there was no other way for the 1541 to announce itself except by talking on this line, and the drive type was auto-detected from what it said.

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: 9-pin high-density D-subminiature, 0.1 inch pitch

facts.label: Cable
facts.value: a flat or twisted pair cable, about 1 m

facts.label: Signal
facts.value: a serial bus, logic levels at 5 V, not RS-232

children.note: It was a 9-pin high-density D-sub on the drive side. On the C64 itself the drive port was a 9-pin D-sub, the same physical connector, and the signals were Commodore serial, not RS-232. Note the parallel with the user port below: the C64's expansion port was a 34-conductor card edge. Three CIA port lines drive the serial bus - ATN out, clock out and data out - each inverted through U8 before reaching the device, and the connector is a 9-pin Mini-D. Not established: the 0.1 inch pitch, the about 1 m cable length, and 5 V logic levels.

children.name: The 34-conductor user port ribbon
children.description: On the back of the C64, a 34-conductor edge connector on a card, which brought out the 6510's eight data lines, twelve address lines, the read and write strobes, the IRQ and NMI lines, the serial and parallel ports, and the 5 V and ground. It was the machine's expansion door, and it was how a disk interface, a printer interface, a sampler or an EPROM programmer reached the CPU. The cable was a flat ribbon with a mylar or tinned-copper conductor, a foil shield and a PVC or polyester jacket.

facts.label: Conductors
facts.value: 34 (17 x 2), 0.1 inch pitch

facts.label: Cable
facts.value: about 20 cm to 30 cm of ribbon, foil-shielded with a drain wire

facts.label: Card edge
facts.value: a gold-plated or nickel-plated PCB edge that plugged into the C64's rear connector

children.note: A ribbon cable of this type is a laminated structure: parallel copper conductors, 0.03-0.05 mm thick, separated by a polyester film, laminated between films, wrapped in a mylar or aluminium-foil shield and a PVC jacket. The foil and the polyester are petroleum and silica products respectively. Whether the 1982 C64 user port card edge was gold-plated or plain nickel is not established; many were simply tin-plated board edge.

children.name: Card-edge and D-sub connectors
children.description: The connectors were gold-plated or nickel-plated brass and copper contacts in a thermoplastic (usually glass-filled nylon or a phenolic) insulator, crimped or soldered to the ribbon. A D-sub has a metal shell (often tinned steel or nickel-plated brass) that both shields the connection and provides the mechanical polarisation that stops anyone plugging it in backwards.

facts.label: Gold
facts.value: 0.05-0.1 microns of hard gold on the contacts, over nickel, from anode slimes

facts.label: Shell
facts.value: brass or steel, nickel-plated, with a ground latch

children.note: The gold on a connector contact is the same anode-slime gold as the bond wire on the 6502. Gold plating on a connector is thin gold over a nickel underplate so the gold does not diffuse into the copper and leave a brittle intermetallic.

children.name: The six-pin cassette port
children.description: The connector that carries both the audio to a tape recorder and the power to a 1541. It is a 6-pin connector, carrying read, write, sense, motor, 5 V and the 9-12 V motor rail. Commodore's own cable turned it into a DIN-style socket that plugged into a consumer cassette recorder, so a C64 could save to a music deck. The same port carried the power for the 1541, which is why a 1541 has no power socket of its own.

facts.label: Signals
facts.value: serial read, serial write, motor on/off, sense, and 5 V plus the 9-12 V rail

facts.label: Cable
facts.value: a moulded 6-pin plug to a 6-pin DIN socket or a cassette-REC-style plug

children.note: The sense pin was how the C64 knew a motorised deck was present, and the motor pin was how it started a consumer recorder. The exact pinout ordering is not established, and a wrong one is worse than none; the functional set of connections is the reliable part.

In the 1992 service manual parts list the back-panel expansion connector is a 44-pin card edge (CN6, C 906100-02) and the drive port is a 9-pin Mini-D (CN8/9, C 251057-01). The 34-conductor figure in this node is not established, nor is the aerial socket type.

root.description: A C64 shipped with no screen. It drove a television set through an RF modulator, saved to a cassette deck through the 1541 drive, and took input from a joystick. Three separate supply chains meet here: the television, the cassette drive, and the connectors that carry the signal between them.

peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.polyethylene.name: Polyethylene from ethylene
peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.polyethylene.description: Polyethylene is polymerised from ethylene, which comes from a steam cracker on naphtha. Where the chlorination route was used (for PVC or for the chloromethane that goes into the foam blowing), the chlorine came from salt electrolysis. Both the polymer and the chlorine are therefore descendants of crude oil and of halite, and both branches meet in the cable jacket.

facts.label: LDPE
facts.value: high-pressure polymerisation, 1000-3000 bar, 200 degrees C, for cable

facts.label: Chlorine
facts.value: salt electrolysis, 2NaCl -> Cl2 + 2Na, at about 3 V and 30-40 degrees C

facts.label: PVC
facts.value: vinyl chloride from ethylene plus chlorine, then polymerised

peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.polyethylene.note: Polyethylene is documented as the most commonly produced plastic, with low-density and high-density forms and many variations, produced in excess of 100 million tonnes a year. Not established: the 1000-3000 bar and 200 C figures as the specification for this grade - the low-density grade is the high-pressure one and that is the route the facts take, but no polymerisation process source was consulted for the numbers - the 2NaCl to Cl2 plus 2Na equation and the claim of about 3 V and 30-40 C for salt electrolysis, where cell voltage and electrolyte temperature are not the same quantity and a chlor-alkali cell runs warm, the vinyl chloride route to PVC, chloromethane as the foam blowing agent, and the Teesside, Gulf Coast and Saudi Arabia works. The two paths meeting in a cable jacket - ethylene from a steam cracker and chlorine from brine electrolysis - is a genuine convergence of the petrochemical and salt chains.

peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.iron.name: Iron from ore or scrap, leached to a ferrous salt
peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.iron.description: Tape pigment iron did not need to be virgin: it was often made from ferrous scrap, mill scale or ore, dissolved in hydrochloric or sulphuric acid to ferrous chloride or ferrous sulphate, then precipitated and oxidised. The ore route, when it was used, was the same hematite or magnetite that goes to a blast furnace, digested in acid rather than reduced in a furnace.

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: hydrochloric acid at 60-90 degrees C, or sulfuric acid at 80-100 degrees C, giving FeCl2 or FeSO4

facts.label: Iron content
facts.value: 72.4% by weight in Fe2O3; the whole 90 m of a C-60 holds only 1-3 g of it

facts.label: Acid route
facts.value: same hematite and magnetite, digested in HCl or H2SO4 rather than reduced with coke

peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.iron.note: One grade of ore fed both the steel of a shadow mask and the oxide on a cassette, by two completely different routes.

peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.surfactan.name: Crystal-habit modifier, fatty acid or sulphonate
peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.surfactan.description: A surfactant, and the reason the word appears on three unrelated branches: what a tape pigment, a printing-ink deinking flotation cell and a chromium dioxide oxidation all have in common is that the chemistry is dominated by an anionic or amphoteric surface-active agent adsorbed on a particle. Crystal habit is controlled by what is adsorbed on the growing face. The pigment industry used a fatty acid or an alkylbenzene sulphonate, or in the classic process a hydrolysed protein or a polyol, adsorbed on the iron oxide as it precipitated so that growth was fastest along one axis. Without it the pigment came out spherical and a cassette tape of the same thickness held a fraction of the data.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: adsorb on the crystal face and inhibit growth there, forcing the acicular habit

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: a percent or so of the pigment weight

peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.surfactan.note: Surfactant choice was one of the genuinely proprietary parts of a tape formulation; both fatty-acid-derived and synthetic-anion-derived chemistries were in use.

peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.chromium.name: Chromium dioxide (Type II pigment)
peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.chromium.description: For high-bias Type II tape, chromium dioxide (CrO2): acicular, 20-50 nm, higher coercivity and higher signal-to-noise than ferrite. It is made by oxidising chromic chloride in the presence of a surfactant under pressure and heat, and was patented and controlled tightly by its Japanese inventors. Chromium came from chromite ore, which is mostly in South Africa and the Soviet bloc.

facts.label: Particle
facts.value: about 0.03 x 0.008 microns, finer than the ferrite

facts.label: Coercivity
facts.value: 40-50 kA/m, high-bias (1200 ns)

facts.label: Curie point
facts.value: about 120 degrees C

facts.label: Oxidation
facts.value: CrO3 reduced to CrO2, or chromic acid oxidised under pressure

peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.chromium.note: Chromium dioxide tape is the Type II high-bias formulation. The 1541 wrote standard-bias, so a Type II tape on a 1541 would have been biased 1200 ns against a 120 ns machine; it would record, but not well. Ferrite, the IEC Type I formulation, was the right tape.

peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.saw.lithiu.name: Spodumene pegmatite ore
peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.saw.lithiu.description: A lithium aluminium silicate, 6.0-7.0% Li2O, that occurs in granitic pegmatites and is mined in enormous tonnages because a lithium battery plant in 1982 needed thousands of tonnes a year. Roasting with sulphuric acid turns it into lithium sulphate, and the impurity that everyone fights is iron.

facts.label: Roast
facts.value: 1050-1100 degrees C with H2SO4 to Li2SO4

facts.label: Iron problem
facts.value: iron from the pegmatite contaminates the carbonate and is removed by precipitation or a calcine

peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.saw.lithiu.note: Spodumene is documented: it is a pyroxene mineral consisting of lithium aluminium inosilicate and is a commercially important source of lithium, occurring in prismatic crystals; the naturally occurring low-temperature form is monoclinic and converts to the tetragonal high-temperature form above 900 C. That conversion figure is the one number here with a source behind it, and it matters because the conversion is what a sulphate roast has to drive through. Not established: the 6.0-7.0% Li2O figure as a pegmatite run-of-mine grade (that is closer to a concentrate figure and the 1-4% claimed in the inputs is the usual head grade), the 1050-1100 C sulphuric acid roast, the precipitation or calcine route for iron removal, and the Greenbushes, Bikita, Tanco and Piedmont works. The demand driver given here is the reason spodumene was mined in large tonnages, but the tonnage and its customer are not documented on this node.

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.name: Lead oxide (litharge), PbO
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.description: The lead in the frit started as galena, PbS, roasted in air to a PbO litharge cake, then smelted. Nothing about this is exotic: it is the same 1900s Parkesine process that made lead-acid battery plates, refined to the point where the oxide is pure white and free of the bismuth and antimony that would grey it.

facts.label: Roast
facts.value: 600-750 degrees C in a fluid-bed or reverberatory furnace, PbS + O2 -> PbO + SO2

facts.label: Smelt
facts.value: sinter plus coke and limestone in a blast furnace to crude lead at 1100-1250 degrees C

facts.label: Refining
facts.value: drossing, then electrolytic refining to 99.99% Pb for litharge

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.note: Named for what it is rather than for where it came from; the galena chain beneath it says where the lead came from. Galena, PbS, is the most important ore of lead, and lead is smelted in a blast furnace from lead sinter with coke, after which the bullion is drossed. Not established: the 600-750 C fluid-bed or reverberatory roast, the 1100-1250 C sinter smelt, the electrolytic refining to 99.99% Pb, and the Herculaneum, Midland and Broken Hill attributions.

peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.geometry.magnets..name: Alnico correction magnet
peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.geometry.magnets..description: An iron-aluminium-nickel alloy with a high Curie point and a hard, brittle, unmachinable structure. Alnico is cast or sintered as a solid block, aged for days at 600-800 C to precipitate its magnetic phase, and then magnetised in a strong field - and it cannot be ground to shape afterwards, so the geometry of the magnet has to be cast in, which is exactly why a set's pincushion and width adjustments are a fixed arrangement of magnets rather than something the customer can trim. The recipe varies across the family and the variation matters for this tree: the original grades were cobalt-free, but the high-coercivity grades of the 1950s onwards added cobalt, titanium and copper, so an Alnico 5 magnet on a 1982 set is an iron-cobalt alloy and the cobalt in it came out of the Copperbelt, not out of the aluminium or the nickel.

facts.label: Cobalt-free grades
facts.value: about 8-12% Al, 15-26% Ni, the rest Fe

facts.label: Cobalt grades
facts.value: Alnico 5 is about 24% Co with 12% Al, 5% Ti and 6% Cu; Alnico 8 is about 35% Co

facts.label: Making
facts.value: cast or sintered, aged 600-800 C to precipitate the magnetic phase, then magnetised

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: brittle and unmachinable, so the magnet's geometry is fixed at the casting and cannot be trimmed

peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.geometry.magnets..note: The composition range across the Alnico family is well documented; which grade a particular 1982 chassis used is not established, and the two differ in whether they contain cobalt at all. The absolute form of the unmachinability claim (no grinding to shape afterwards) goes beyond the cited page, which documents brittleness and cast-in complex shapes.

peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.geometry.magnets..name: Samarium-cobalt correction magnet
peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.geometry.magnets..description: A rare-earth permanent magnet with roughly twice the energy product of Alnico from a fraction of the volume, made by sintering or bonding finely divided samarium-cobalt powder and magnetising it. Its coercivity comes from samarium's affinity for cobalt, which holds the grains from rotating back into alignment, so the magnet resists demagnetisation far better than Alnico and does not need the iron it replaced. That is a real advantage on a deflection magnet, and it is exactly why the material was developed for this job and then priced out of a domestic set: samarium oxide was one of the more expensive rare-earth fractions, so the magnet cost was set by the separation plant rather than by the metallurgy.

facts.label: Energy product
facts.value: roughly twice Alnico's from a fraction of the volume

facts.label: Coercivity
facts.value: samarium's affinity for cobalt holds the grains against demagnetisation, so no iron is needed

facts.label: Cost driver
facts.value: samarium oxide is one of the more expensive rare-earth fractions, so price is set by the separation plant

facts.label: 1982 uptake
facts.value: too new and too expensive for a domestic set; standard in small deflection magnets by the 1990s

peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.geometry.magnets..note: Which correction magnets in which 1982 sets were in fact samarium-cobalt is not established; the node records the material and its economics rather than a claim about a particular chassis. Established on the cited page: the SmCo material itself (sintered rare-earth magnet, high coercivity and temperature stability, energy products 14-33 MG·Oe). Not established there: the samarium-oxide cost multiple and the standard-1990s-uptake claim.

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.silver.name: Silver activator
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.silver.description: The blue ZnS is activated by silver at a fraction of a percent, supplied as silver nitrate. Silver itself came from argentite and from the anode slimes that accumulate in electrolytic copper refining, which is where most of the world's silver of the era was actually recovered.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: about 0.05-0.1 wt% Ag

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.silver.note: Silver for phosphors was one of the smaller industrial users, but the same tonne went into contacts and brazing alloys.

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.gold.name: Gold activator
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.gold.description: The green ZnS:Au needs a discrete gold level about 0.1% down. The gold came from cyanide leaching of refractory ore and from the anode slimes of copper refining, refined by the Wohlwill process to 99.99% and dissolved in aqua regia.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: about 0.05-0.2 wt% Au

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.gold.note: A television green phosphor contains a genuinely tiny amount of gold. Several tens of thousands of colour tubes a year is a real, if small, consumer of the metal.

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.copper.name: Copper activator
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.copper.description: Copper, usually added as copper oxide, deepens the green and creates the donor level that the blue's co-activator needs. It came from copper concentrate, smelted and electrorefined to 99.99% copper and converted to CuO.
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.copper.note: Copper(II) oxide, CuO, is documented: it is a black solid, one of the two stable oxides of copper, and a product of copper mining that is the precursor to many other copper compounds. That is the substance this node names. Not established: that copper is the activator that deepens the green and creates the donor level the blue co-activator needs, that it was supplied to the phosphor maker as the oxide rather than as a copper salt or a copper concentrate, the sulphuric acid step, and the Chuquicamata, Butte and Zambia attributions. The activator roles of Ag, Au, Sb and Eu in the P22 phosphors are far better documented than copper, which is why this node is thinner than its neighbours.

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.europium.name: Europium oxide
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.europium.description: Europium is the activator that makes a television's red, and it was the one rare earth that a mass market paid for. It is used at a loading of a few tenths of a percent in the host lattice, where the Eu3+ ion's sharp 610 nm 4f-4f transition gives a narrow-band red that the zinc sulphide host itself cannot. Two red formulations were in service in 1982 and the trade between them was chromaticity against stability: CaS:Eu gave the better red but is hygroscopic and had to be protected from moisture, while europium-doped ZnS was more forgiving and slightly less saturated. The oxide itself arrives at 99.9% from the rare-earth separation plant, having begun as a few tenths of a percent of a ton of concentrate.

facts.label: Emission
facts.value: about 610 nm, Eu3+ 4f-4f transition

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: a few tenths of a percent of the host lattice

facts.label: The two 1982 reds
facts.value: CaS:Eu, better chromaticity but hygroscopic; Eu-doped ZnS, more stable and less saturated

facts.label: Not the scarce thing
facts.value: bastnasite runs 6-9% rare-earth oxides, so the ore was milled in large tonnage to get a few hundred tonnes of europium oxide

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.europium.note: Confidence is low on the formulation, not on the supply: the red formulation of any particular 1982 tube was proprietary, and which manufacturer used CaS:Eu against Eu-doped ZnS is not established - both were in service. The europium supply side is well documented, and the same concentrate supplied the samarium in the correction magnets.

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.batc.name: Alkali-free batch: silica, alumina, boron
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.batc.description: Where the funnel batch leaned on lead and alkali for its expansion match, the panel batch deliberately excluded sodium and potassium and got its properties from silica, alumina and boric oxide plus a small amount of barium to suppress solarisation under the phosphor firing. It is the same silica sand as the funnel, but a batch designed to be unfriendly to sodium.
inputs: antimony or arsenic as a fining agent

facts.label: Na2O + K2O
facts.value: held below about 1% for an alkali-free panel glass

facts.label: Melt
facts.value: same 1380-1500 degrees C tank furnace as the funnel

facts.label: Solarisation
facts.value: the phosphor firing at 430-450 degrees C can darken a glass with too much alkali; barium and antimony suppressed it

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.batc.note: The alumina in a panel batch is refractory-grade alumina from the Bayer process, not the four-nines rolled foil used behind the phosphor; metal.alumina, the canonical alumina in this tree, is the ingredient it takes.

peripheral.plug.userport.pvc.name: PVC jacket and polyester film from crude oil
peripheral.plug.userport.pvc.description: The ribbon's jacket is PVC (from ethylene and salt-derived chlorine) and its insulation between conductors is polyester film (from the same PET chain as the cassette tape base). Both are grandchildren of crude oil, and both are the same two chemistries already traced elsewhere in this tree.

facts.label: PVC
facts.value: suspension-polymerised, 57 degrees C, plasticised with a phthalate ester

facts.label: Plasticiser
facts.value: DOP or DINP, itself from an oxo process on butanol, which is from propylene

peripheral.plug.userport.pvc.note: The PVC takes metal.salt-brine, the canonical salt, as an ingredient.

peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.name: Acicular iron oxide pigment
peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.description: The magnetic pigment is acicular gamma-iron(III) oxide, gamma-Fe2O3: needle-shaped crystals about 0.3 microns long by 0.08 microns across by 0.01 thick, an aspect ratio of about 3 to 5. It is precipitated from an iron(II) salt by oxidising with air while a surfactant is present, and the surfactant is what forces the crystals to grow as needles instead of spheres. That morphology is the whole reason a cassette can hold what it holds: the long axis lines up with the tape's direction of travel and the short axis resists it.

facts.label: Particle
facts.value: about 0.3 x 0.08 x 0.01 microns, aspect ratio 3-5

facts.label: Crystal
facts.value: gamma-Fe2O3, maghemite, tetragonal

facts.label: Coercivity
facts.value: 25-30 kA/m standard, up to 40-50 kA/m with cobalt modification

facts.label: Remanence
facts.value: about 0.25-0.3 T

facts.label: Precipitation
facts.value: Fe(II) salt oxidised by air at 50-80 degrees C with a surfactant

peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.note: The pigment is made from iron ore or from ferrous scrap by dissolving it in hydrochloric or sulphuric acid to a ferrous (FeII) salt, precipitating the hydrate with a caustic, and then oxidising it slowly to gamma-Fe2O3 while a surfactant or a nucleating protein steers the crystal habit. The chromium-dioxide pigment for Type II tape was made by oxidising chromium chloride in the presence of a similar surfactant and was a higher coercivity, more stable formulation.
places: Japan (TDK, TDK's TPIO2 chrome and iron oxides)

peripheral.cassette.tape.dispersion.name: The dispersion: pigment, binder, dispersant
peripheral.cassette.tape.dispersion.description: The pigment was not coated as a powder. It was dispersed in a binder so that the needles separate and stay separated, and then magnetically oriented on the film. A typical binder was a cellulose lacquer, an acrylic or polyurethane, dissolved in a solvent such as toluene, xylene or methyl ethyl ketone; in the 1970s and early 1980s there was also a water-based polyurethane dispersion. The dispersant was a surfactant or a phosphate ester that wets the oxide surface so the needles do not clump back together. The pigment and the binder are combined and then refined on a three-roll mill or a sand mill, working the agglomerates apart from a few tens of microns down to a few microns at 50-70% solids, until the dispersion is smooth. Dispersion quality set the noise floor of the finished tape, because a clump of pigment is a defect that scatters the recording.
inputs: cellulose lacquer or acrylic or polyurethane binder

facts.label: Solvent
facts.value: toluene, xylene or MEK; water-based polyurethane came in through the 1980s

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: a few percent by weight; a cellulose or acrylic lacquer

facts.label: Pigment loading
facts.value: about 60-75% by volume of the dried coating

facts.label: Milling
facts.value: three-roll or sand mill, gap from tens of microns down to a few, 50-70% solids

peripheral.cassette.tape.dispersion.note: Toluene and xylene are aromatics from the same naphtha cracking that feeds styrene. The binder chemistry for magnetic tape was for decades one of the most closely guarded industrial secrets; the general class (cellulose lacquer, then acrylic, then polyurethane) is reliable, the specific recipes are not.

peripheral.cassette.tape.pad.materials.name: Felt and the stainless spring
peripheral.cassette.tape.pad.materials.description: The pad was wool felt or a bonded polyester fibre web about a millimetre thick, glued to a stainless steel leaf spring in a plastic carrier. Wool felt is carded wool fibre matted and pressed; the spring was a 300-series stainless, so the iron came from the blast furnace and the chromium from chromite, the same chromite as the chrome plating on a telescopic antenna.

facts.label: Felt
facts.value: about 0.5-1 mm of matted wool or synthetic fibre

facts.label: Spring
facts.value: 0.15-0.3 mm stainless strip, giving a few tenths of a newton

peripheral.cassette.tape.pad.materials.note: A strip of 300-series stainless is made of blast-furnace iron and ferrochrome, and the spring is chrome-plated, so both are ingredients of the pad rather than things it contains.

peripheral.cassette.tape.shell.abs.name: Shell material: polystyrene or ABS
peripheral.cassette.tape.shell.abs.description: A cassette shell is thin and needs to hold a dimension, so it was moulded from general-purpose polystyrene (cheap, brittle, easy to mould) or from ABS for a stiffer shell. Audio tapes were conventionally clear or smoke polystyrene or ABS; computer and C64 tapes were frequently the same shells, since nothing about the shell distinguished them.

facts.label: Wall
facts.value: 1-2 mm

facts.label: Moulding
facts.value: injection, 200-240 degrees C, a very fast cycle for a thin shell

peripheral.cassette.tape.shell.abs.note: ABS is documented: a thermoplastic terpolymer of styrene, acrylonitrile and butadiene in common use since the 1950s, amorphous with no definitive melting point because of varying chain lengths and degrees of cross-linking, with a glass transition temperature of approximately 105 C, and usable between about -20 and 80 C for the majority of applications. That last range is the useful part here, because a cassette shell works near room temperature and has no thermal duty. Not established: that the shell was ABS rather than clear or smoke general-purpose polystyrene, the 1-2 mm wall, the 200-240 C injection moulding temperature, and the Japan, Europe and United States attributions. The claim that a shell needed to hold a dimension, and therefore that the stiffer of the two polymers was the one chosen, is an engineering argument; a shell could equally be a thin polystyrene moulding with ribs.

peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb.glass.name: E-glass fibre from silica sand
peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb.glass.description: The reinforcement is a textile of drawn glass filament: silica sand is melted in a bushing at 1400 degrees C, drawn to a fibre a few microns across, and woven into cloth. It is the same silica as the tank window glass, run through a different furnace.

facts.label: Fibre diameter
facts.value: 5-24 microns, woven into a cloth of about 0.1-0.2 mm thickness

facts.label: Function
facts.value: raises the laminate's dimensional stability and its solder-heat resistance

facts.label: E-glass composition
facts.value: about 73% SiO2, 16% CaO, 6% B2O3

facts.label: Drawing
facts.value: about 100 microns at the bushing, drawn to 5-24 microns

peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb.glass.note: The same E-glass concept was invented for the printed circuit board and, by 1982, was also being pulled as optical fibre for telecommunications. Both start as melted quartz sand drawn to a fine filament. Glass fibre is the board industry's reinforcement; optical fibre is the telecommunications industry's, off the same melted quartz sand.

peripheral.cassette.deck.head.core.name: Permalloy or ferrite core
peripheral.cassette.deck.head.core.description: The gap has to be made with both faces flat and parallel to a micron or so across a couple of millimetres, which ferrite does well by lapping and permalloy does well by etching. A high-permeability nickel-iron alloy, permalloy, gives the inductance needed for the playback winding; the mu-metal shield can around the front suppresses external fields.
inputs: nickel iron (permalloy, 79% Ni) or MnZn ferrite

facts.label: Permalloy
facts.value: about 79% Ni, 17% Fe, 4% Mo/Cu; permeability about 20,000-100,000

facts.label: Mu-metal
facts.value: about 77% Ni, 20% Fe, 2% Cu, annealed in hydrogen, permeability about 100,000

facts.label: Gap
facts.value: 1 micrometre, made by sputtering a spacer or by bonding two lapped faces

peripheral.cassette.deck.head.core.note: The nickel comes from the same nickel chain as the CRT grid foil. Mu-metal's nickel content is higher than permalloy's and it must be annealed in hydrogen at about 1100 degrees C to develop its permeability.

peripheral.cassette.deck.head.winding.name: Lacquered copper wire, figure-eight
peripheral.cassette.deck.head.winding.description: The winding was a fine enamelled (lacquered) copper wire, typically 40 AWG, a few hundred to a couple of thousand turns, wound so that it sits astride the gap with two halves that see the drive motor's stray field in opposite directions. The hum-cancelling figure-eight was the reason a 1541 did not pick up the buzz of its own motor. The lacquer itself is the same polyurethane-imide over a polyester base as a television yoke winding.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 0.1-0.13 mm enamelled copper

facts.label: Hum cancelling
facts.value: figure-eight: two coils in series, opposed

peripheral.cassette.deck.head.winding.note: Not established: 40 AWG or 0.1-0.13 mm enamelled copper, the figure-eight hum-cancelling winding, and the turns count for a 1541 read/write head.

peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.rotor.name: Sintered ferrite permanent magnet rotor
peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.rotor.description: The rotor is a ferrite or Alnico magnet with fine teeth machined or ground onto its circumference, magnetised radially or axially. A ferrite magnet is barium or strontium ferrite, the same material as a speaker magnet; a stepper rotor is a small ring of it.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: sintered barium or strontium ferrite, or an Alnico 5 or 8 segment

facts.label: Coercivity
facts.value: about 160-250 kA/m for ferrite, enough to survive demagnetising the two stator fields

facts.label: Tooth finish
facts.value: sintered and diamond-ground, teeth concentric to a few microns

peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.rotor.note: Barium ferrite is documented: barium hexaferrite, BaFe12O19, and related ferrite materials are components in magnetic stripe cards and loudspeaker magnets. A hybrid stepper rotor is the same material in a toothed ring, so the choice is documented. Not established: strontium ferrite as the alternative in this position, the 160-250 kA/m coercivity figure, an Alnico 5 or 8 segmented rotor as an alternative construction, sinter-and-diamond-grinding of the teeth to a few microns of concentricity, magnetisation being radial or axial, and the Japan and Netherlands works. The requirement is real and checkable in one respect: the rotor has to survive being brought near demagnetising by the two stator fields, which is what the coercivity figure is about. Which of the three magnet families a particular drive used is not documented, and a small ferrite ring and a cast Alnico rotor are not interchangeable in cost or in volume.

peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.housing.name: End bell steel and sintered bronze bushings
peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.housing.description: The stamped steel end bells came off the same low-carbon sheet as the shadow mask and the speaker basket. The bushings were sintered bronze, a copper-tin alloy made by pressing bronze powder and sintering it in a reducing atmosphere so it had a connected pore structure that held oil. Copper and tin both feature elsewhere in this branch.

facts.label: Bronze
facts.value: about 85-90% Cu, 8-10% Sn, 1-2% Zn, pressed and sintered

facts.label: Porosity
facts.value: about 10-25% interconnected pores to hold lubricant

peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.housing.note: Stamped end bells are made of cold-reduced sheet steel and the bushings are made of copper and tin, so a motor housing draws on the steel and the tin rather than containing them.

peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.gold-wire.name: Gold bonding wire from the anode slimes
peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.gold-wire.description: The 6502 was a 40-pin DIP with gold or tinned copper wires ball-bonded or wedge-bonded from the die pads to the lead frame. Gold came almost entirely from the anode slimes of copper electrolytic refining, and a modest 40-pin DIP of the period had a few milligrams of it.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 0.7-1.5 mil (18-38 micron) gold, or 1-2 mil tinned copper

peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.gold-wire.note: Gold is documented as dense, soft, malleable and ductile, resistant to most acids and to reaction with most chemicals, and its malleability, ductility and corrosion resistance together with electrical conductivity have led to its continued use in corrosion-resistant electrical connectors in all types of computerized devices. That backs the bonding-wire role. Not established: the 0.7-1.5 mil (18-38 micron) wire diameter and the 1-2 mil tinned copper alternative, ball bonding against wedge bonding as the technique of the period, and the quantity of gold in a 40-pin package - a few milligrams is a plausible order of magnitude for a bond-wire package, but no teardown was done. Gold from the anode slimes of copper refining is a real and very large share of supply; it is the same silver and gold that lead smelting recovers from bullion dross, so the metal arrives here by two quite separate routes.

peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.silicon.m.name: Epoxy mould compound, silica-filled
peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.silicon.m.description: The black or off-white plastic that a chip is set in. It is an epoxy novolac resin filled to about 70% with ground fused silica, with a cure promoter and a mould release. The silica filler is what stops the encapsulant from shrinking and cracking the die during cure, and it comes from the same kind of sand as the glass batch.

facts.label: Filler
facts.value: about 70% by weight ground silica, angular, a few microns

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 175 degrees C for several minutes, transfer or injection mould

peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.silicon.m.note: The filler is deliberately angular and fused rather than spherical: the sharp interlocking particles give a high mechanical strength and a low water uptake, which is what kept moisture out of the die.

peripheral.tv.mains.fuse.material.name: Glass cartridge and silver fuse wire
peripheral.tv.mains.fuse.material.description: A small glass or ceramic cartridge containing a link of silver or of a fusible alloy such as a lead-bismuth-tin eutectic, in a sand or chalk packing that quenched the arc when the link melted. The glass was soda-lime, drawn as a tube and sealed with an end cap.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 3-4 A, 250 V, time delay on larger sets

facts.label: Fusing element
facts.value: silver wire, or a 500 degree C fusible alloy

peripheral.tv.mains.fuse.material.note: A fuse is documented: its essential component is a metal wire or strip that melts when too much current flows through it, and it is a sacrificial device that becomes an open circuit once it has operated. Silver is documented as having the highest electrical conductivity of any element, which is why it was chosen for a fusing element. Not established: that a 1982 set used silver wire rather than a fusible alloy, the 3-4 A 250 V time-delay rating, quartz sand or chalk as the arc-quenching packing, soda-lime glass as the cartridge tube, and the IEC pattern and Japanese attributions. The lead-bismuth-tin eutectic named here as the alternative is one of several low-melting alloys used for exactly this purpose; the particular alloy is not documented.

peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.name: Coaxial or twin-lead antenna lead
peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.description: RG-59 or RG-6 coax: a copper or tinned copper braid, a polyethylene or PTFE dielectric, and a solid copper centre conductor. RG-59 is 52 ohm and was what an indoor or a bench lead of the era was. The alternative was 300 ohm flat twin-lead, which matched indoor dipoles and did not need coax. The polyethylene in the coax came from ethylene, which came from the cracker, which came from naphtha and from crude.

facts.label: RG-59
facts.value: 52 ohm, about 6.5 mm outside diameter

facts.label: Twin-lead
facts.value: 300 ohm, 2 x 1.2 mm polyethylene-insulated conductors

facts.label: PE dielectric
facts.value: chemical blowing makes a foam, or solid PE

peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.note: Coaxial cable is documented: an inner centre conductor surrounded by a concentric conducting shield with the two separated by a dielectric, it is a type of unbalanced transmission line used to carry high-frequency electrical signals with low losses, it differs from other shielded cables because the dimensions of the cable and its connectors are controlled to give a precise, constant conductor spacing, and that separation from twin-lead is exactly the point this node makes about the alternative. Not established: RG-59 at 52 ohm and about 6.5 mm outside diameter, RG-6, 300 ohm flat twin-lead at 2 x 1.2 mm polyethylene-insulated conductors as the indoor dipole alternative, chemical blowing to make foam polyethylene as against solid PE, and that RG-59 was the era bench or indoor lead. The characteristic impedance and outside diameter of RG-59 are published cable specifications, but they were not confirmed against a cable datasheet here.

peripheral.tv.controls.switch.silver.name: Silver-plated switch contacts
peripheral.tv.controls.switch.silver.description: Mains switch and rotary tuner contacts were silver-plated brass or copper, because silver has the highest conductivity of any metal and does not oxidise. Silver plating was applied from a cyanide or an acid bath, and the silver itself came overwhelmingly from the anode slimes of copper refining.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: about 2.5-25 microns of silver

facts.label: Life
facts.value: the contacts of a 1982 TV tuner were good for 10,000-20,000 insertions

peripheral.tv.controls.switch.silver.note: Silver is documented as having the highest electrical conductivity of any element, and gold is documented as dissolving in alkaline solutions of cyanide, which is used in both mining and electroplating - so cyanide plating is an established route for both metals. Not established: that mains switch and rotary tuner contacts were silver-plated rather than silver-clad or merely plated with a cheaper metal, the 2.5-25 micron thickness, and the claim that a 1982 tuner was good for 10,000-20,000 insertions. Plating thickness in the few microns is ordinary for a precious-metal contact, but the figure is a specification range rather than an observation. The silver in this branch comes from the anode slimes of copper refining, which is the same source documented for the phosphor silver and for the fuse wire.

peripheral.tv.speaker.cone.name: Paper pulp cone
peripheral.tv.speaker.cone.description: The cone is a paper pulp: refined wood fibre pressed wet into a shaped blank and dried, giving a light, stiff, cheap diaphragm. It is essentially the same material as a paper bag, which is why it creases if you poke it. A small set used a paper cone; a later or better one a woven or moulded polypropylene cone.

facts.label: Forming
facts.value: slurry of kraft pulp pressed in a hot press and dried in a kiln or on a belt

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: a few grams for a 3.5 inch cone

peripheral.tv.speaker.cone.note: The sound cone is one of the few parts of a television that starts as a tree. Pulp is wood reduced to fibre, and the fibre is from softwood, which is a renewable, not a geological, raw material. It is the one leaf in this branch that is not dug out of the ground. The cone is one of the three common sound radiation systems, and driver diaphragms are made of paper or composite materials. Not established: the wet-pressed kraft pulp route, the kiln or belt drying, and a few grams for a 3.5 inch cone.

peripheral.tv.speaker.magnet.name: Ferrite magnet
peripheral.tv.speaker.magnet.description: A ring or cup magnet of barium or strontium ferrite, sintered and magnetised across the gap. Barium ferrite needed barium carbonate, which is why barite mining also fed speakers. Ferrite, not Alnico, was the standard by 1982 because it was cheap and had a higher coercivity.

facts.label: Energy product
facts.value: about 3-4 x 10^3 kJ/m3 for barium ferrite

facts.label: Forming
facts.value: pressed and sintered at 1200-1250 degrees C

peripheral.tv.speaker.magnet.note: The barium here is the same element as in the CRT getter (barite for barium metal). Different ore routes, same element. Strontium ferrite was taking over by the late 1980s because strontium carbonate is cheaper than barium.

peripheral.tv.chassis.video.ic.die.name: Silicon wafer, P-type
peripheral.tv.chassis.video.ic.die.description: The wafer this die is cut from is a slice of 99.99% silicon: p-type boron-doped substrate with n-epitaxy grown on top for the bipolar transistors, then oxidised, patterned and metallised. A 4-micron process of 1982 ran on a 100 or 125 mm wafer, with 150 mm arriving in 1983. The difference between this wafer and the one in the EHT rectifier is the epitaxy and the oxide, not the feedstock: both come out of the same trichlorosilane and Siemens chain from quartz and metallurgical silicon.
inputs: oxygen and steam for the oxides

facts.label: Wafer
facts.value: 100 or 125 mm; 150 mm wafers were arriving in 1983

facts.label: Resistivity
facts.value: 1-20 ohm cm p-type substrate

facts.label: Epitaxy
facts.value: n+ 1000-2000 nm at 1100-1200 degrees C

peripheral.tv.chassis.video.ic.die.note: What is specific to a wafer, as against the wafer in the EHT rectifier, is the epitaxy and the oxide, and those are what the facts here give numbers for. Not established: the 4 micron 1982 process, the 100 or 125 mm wafer with 150 mm arriving in 1983, the 1-20 ohm cm p-type substrate, and the n+ 1000-2000 nm epitaxy at 1100-1200 C.

peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.saw.lithiu.name: Lithium niobate wafer
peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.saw.lithiu.description: The acoustic medium. Spodumene (LiAlSi2O6) ore is beneficiated and converted to lithium carbonate by sulphuric acid roasting; the carbonate is reacted with niobium pentoxide from pyrochlore (columbite-tantalite) tantalum residue in a lithium hydroxide or carbonate flux at 1000-1200 degrees C to grow Czochralski crystals of LiNbO3, which are sliced and polished to a 0.25-1 mm wafer. In 1982 much of the world's LiNbO3 came from Japanese and Chinese plants, with the tantalum industry as the source of the columbite residue.

facts.label: Czochralski growth
facts.value: about 1100-1200 degrees C, from a charge of carbonate flux, pulled at 2-20 mm/h

facts.label: Piezoelectric coefficient
facts.value: large, about 6-30 C/m2 per N depending on cut

facts.label: Acoustic velocity
facts.value: about 6000 m/s along the surface

facts.label: Wafer
facts.value: 0.25-0.5 mm, mirror-polished on both faces

places: Bikita, Zimbabwe and Tanco, Manitoba for spodumene
peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.saw.lithiu.note: Lithium niobate is documented as a synthetic salt of niobium, lithium and oxygen whose single crystals are an important material for piezoelectric sensors and for optical applications, and it is a real commercial crystal grown by the Czochralski process. Not established: that lithium niobate rather than piezoelectric quartz or a tantalum-lithium niobate or germanate was the acoustic medium in a 1982 television trap filter, the 1100-1200 C growth and the 2-20 mm/h pull rate, the 6-30 C/m2 per N piezoelectric coefficient and the 6000 m/s surface velocity, the 0.25-0.5 mm wafer, the columbite residue and tantalum residue sourcing described here, and the Takasaki, Yibin and Jiangxi works. The claim that the tantalum industry was the source of the columbite residue is an industrial inference, not a documented statement. Surface acoustic wave devices are the application; the material choice inside one is a design decision.

peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.core.name: Ferrite E-I or C core
peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.core.description: An open-frame core of MnZn ferrite or powdered iron with a gapped section. The gap is deliberate: the flyback has to store a lot of field energy and be reset every line. The core is wound on a bobbin, then potted in epoxy so the 15 kHz and 25 kV windings cannot move.

facts.label: Core size
facts.value: roughly 40-60 mm across for a 13 inch set

facts.label: Gap
facts.value: 0.1-0.5 mm, often a paper or epoxy gap

facts.label: Winding
facts.value: primary 40-100 turns, HV 10,000-25,000 turns

peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.core.note: The flyback transformer is documented: also called a line output transformer, it was designed to generate high-voltage sawtooth signals at a relatively high frequency, and it is used extensively in switched-mode power supplies for both low and over-10 kV outputs. That establishes the device and its function. Not established: MnZn ferrite as the 1982 core material rather than a powdered iron or a ferrite of another grade, the 40-60 mm core size, the 0.1-0.5 mm gap and its paper or epoxy construction, the 40-100 turn primary and the 10,000-25,000 turn high-voltage winding, the epoxy potting, and the Japan, Taiwan and Germany works. Ferrite and powdered iron cores are both documented materials today; which one a particular 1982 set used is a service-manual detail that was not consulted.

peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.anode-lead.sea.name: The glass-to-metal seal materials
peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.anode-lead.sea.description: The anode button was a nickel or Kovar cup frit-sealed into the funnel wall, and the external cap was moulded silicone rubber. The seal frit was the same lead borosilicate as the panel seal, which is why the button had to be fired at the same 430-460 degrees C in the same continuous kiln as the tube.

facts.label: Seal
facts.value: frit printed and fired at 430-460 degrees C

facts.label: External cap
facts.value: silicone rubber, rated for the full EHT

peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.anode-lead.sea.note: Glass-to-metal sealing is documented, and it states the two conditions this seal depends on: the molten glass must be capable of wetting the metal in order to form a tight bond, and the thermal expansion of the glass and metal must be closely matched so that the seal remains solid as the assembly cools. It also records that a seal whose metal has the larger expansion coefficient breaks on cooling. That is the whole physics of an anode button. Not established: lead borosilicate as the specific frit and any match to the panel seal frit, nickel or Kovar as the button material, the 430-460 C firing, the continuous belt kiln shared with the tube, the 3-6 mm silicone cap, and the St. Louis and Japan works. The document names only a few suppliers of specialty sealing glass, and it does not describe a television tube.

peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.hv-rectifier.s.name: High-purity silicon and polysilicon
peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.hv-rectifier.s.description: The EHT rectifier needed silicon of 200-1000 ohm cm with very low oxygen, because the junction had to hold 25 kV without leakage or breakdown. High-purity silicon is made by reducing trichlorosilane or silane, in the trichlorosilane route, from metallurgical silicon, which itself is made in a submerged arc furnace from quartz and coke.

facts.label: Metallurgical silicon
facts.value: submerged arc furnace, 1800-2000 degrees C, 98-99% Si

facts.label: Triclorosilane
facts.value: Si + 3HCl -> SiHCl3 + 2H2, 300 degrees C

facts.label: SiC deposition
facts.value: 1100-1200 degrees C, Siemens process, trichlorosilane plus H2

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 9-11 N for power devices

peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.hv-rectifier.s.note: The process converts metallurgical-grade silicon of about 98% purity to trichlorosilane and then to silicon, removing transition metal and dopant impurities; polysilicon can be as much as 99.9999% pure and metallurgical grade is 95-99%. Not established: the 200-1000 ohm cm resistivity and low oxygen needed to hold 25 kV, the 9-11 N figure for power devices, and the Jamestown, Jersey and Freiburg attributions.

peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.core.name: MnZn ferrite or powdered iron core
peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.core.description: The yoke has to carry a 15 kHz sawtooth of several amps and not heat up, so the core is a high-permeability ferrite or a bonded powdered iron (ferrite dust in a phenolic or rubber binder), pressed and sintered. Ferrite is MnO with ZnO added to raise the saturation flux; powdered iron (Ferralium-type alloys) was used where saturation beat loss mattered.

facts.label: MnZn ferrite
facts.value: used up to about 100-200 kHz, saturation about 0.3-0.4 T

facts.label: Powdered iron
facts.value: sintered alloy, saturation about 0.6-0.8 T, higher loss

facts.label: Pressed and fired
facts.value: 100-200 MPa then 1100-1250 degrees C

peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.core.note: Ferrite is documented as an iron-oxide magnetic ceramic that is not electrically conductive, which is exactly why it suppresses eddy currents in a core, and soft ferites are documented as the material for efficient cores in transformers, inductors and antennas. A ferrite yoke is therefore a coherent choice. Not established: that a 1982 set used MnZn rather than MnNi or a bonded powdered iron, the 0.3-0.4 T saturation flux, the 100-200 MPa pressing load and the 1100-1250 C firing, the 0.6-0.8 T saturation claimed for powdered iron, the Ferralium-type alloy designation, and the Japan, Netherlands and United States works. The nickel oxide listed as an input does not belong to an MnZn ferrite; nickel oxide is an input to MnNi and to nickel-zinc ferrites.

peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.geometry.magnets.name: Correction magnets on the tube neck
peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.geometry.magnets.description: A pair of small magnets sitting on the neck of the tube, arranged to tilt the deflection field and move the deflection centre without touching the geometry circuit. In a 1982 domestic set these were almost always cast Alnico; the high-performance alternative, a samarium-cobalt magnet, cost several times as much for no benefit a consumer could see on a 13 inch screen, and only became standard in the small deflection magnets of the 1990s. The mass in either case is a few grams.

facts.label: 1982 choice
facts.value: cast Alnico, or a small ferrite

facts.label: Why not Sm-Co
facts.value: several times the cost for no visible benefit on a 13 inch screen

peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.geometry.magnets.note: A correction magnet is Alnico or Sm-Co. Europium is a separate use of the same concentrate: it is a phosphor activator, not a magnet alloy. Of the commonly available magnets only rare-earth magnets such as neodymium and samarium-cobalt are stronger than alnico, which supports the cost-versus-benefit argument this node makes. Not established: that 1982 domestic sets almost always used cast alnico rather than a small ferrite, the samarium-cobalt cost multiple, and the Japan and Netherlands attributions.

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.kovar.name: Kovar, the Fe-Ni-Co lead-in glass match
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.kovar.description: A 29% Ni, 17% Co, 53% Fe alloy whose expansion matches a lead borosilicate glass. It is how the anode lead and the stem get sealed into the glass funnel without cracking the tube wall, and it is the same idea as the frit seal but metal instead of glass.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 53% Fe, 29% Ni, 17% Co, expansion about 5 x 10^-6 / K

facts.label: Use
facts.value: frit-sealing the anode stem and the heater stem

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.kovar.note: Kovar was standard in every CRT factory and its own supply chain came from nickel and iron rather than anything exotic. An alloy is made of its metals, so it draws on blast-furnace iron, electrolytic cathode nickel, and cobalt metal, for which no canonical node exists anywhere in this tree yet. Cobalt was a genuinely scarce metal in 1982 and set the price of the alloy.

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.cathode.nio-cr.name: Nickel-chromium cathode base metal
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.cathode.nio-cr.description: The cup that carries the emitting coating: a nickel-chromium alloy, about 82% Ni with 18% Cr, spun or deep drawn to a shallow cup. The alloy is chosen because it does not react with the alkaline-earth oxides fired onto it and does not outgas badly in a vacuum that has to hold for the life of the tube. It is an alloy, not a pure metal, so it draws on the blast furnace for its iron as well as on the nickel refinery.

facts.label: Base alloy
facts.value: Ni-Cr, about 82% Ni with 18% Cr, spun or deep drawn

facts.label: Sheet gauge
facts.value: 0.15-0.3 mm, from the same nickel stock as the grid foils

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.cathode.nio-cr.note: The cup metal and the emitting coating are two different substances. The barium, strontium and calcium carbonates that become the BaO-SrO-CaO coating belong to the cathode, not to the alloy, so the alloy is only the metal the cup is formed from.

peripheral.tv.crt.mask.steel.name: Cold-reduced low-carbon sheet steel
peripheral.tv.crt.mask.steel.description: Low-carbon sheet with very little residual stress, because a mask that warped would break the geometry. It comes off the hot strip mill, is cold-reduced to 0.1-0.2 mm in a reversing mill, annealed in a hydrogen or nitrogen atmosphere, and slit.

facts.label: Carbon
facts.value: under 0.1% (1008/1010 grade)

facts.label: Yield strength
facts.value: about 200-350 MPa cold-reduced

facts.label: Annealing
facts.value: 700-800 degrees C, batch or continuous

peripheral.tv.crt.mask.steel.note: Cold rolling as a route is documented, and cold-reduced low-carbon sheet is the right family of material for a shadow mask: the mask has to hold a slot geometry through a stress-relieving heat treatment, so residual stress and flatness matter more than strength. Not established: the 1008 or 1010 grade designation and the sub-0.1% carbon, the 200-350 MPa yield strength for that grade, the hydrogen or nitrogen annealing atmosphere, the 700-800 C annealing temperature, the 0.1-0.2 mm final gauge, and the Gary, Kawasaki and Itaqui works. A mask alloy that matched the panel expansion was a real problem, which is why bimetallic and electroformed nickel masks exist at all; a single low-carbon steel sheet is the 1982 answer, but the specific grade is a reconstruction.

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.aluminium.name: Vacuum-deposited aluminium backing layer
