peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.aluminium.description: The single most important trick in a CRT, and a layer rather than an operation: a 0.1-0.5 micron aluminium film, 0.1-0.5 microns thick and better than 99.99% pure, evaporated onto the inside of the printed phosphor. Without it, ambient light reflecting off the phosphor coating would lift the black level and the picture would look grey in a lit room. Aluminium is transparent to 25 kV electrons and mirror-reflective to visible light, so light emitted by the phosphor passes out through the glass while room light is bounced back in and trapped. It is deposited in a vacuum evaporator - 0.1-0.15 mm foil pinched onto a feed wire and flash-evaporated off resistive or e-beam filaments at about 1500 degrees C, at better than 1e-4 mbar and typically 1e-5 - and a thin dust-protection layer of a silicate or organosilicon compound is vapour-deposited on top afterwards, because bare aluminium under 25 kV slowly forms aluminium oxide.

facts.label: Vacuum
facts.value: better than 1e-4 mbar, typically 1e-5

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 0.1-0.5 microns

facts.label: Foil
facts.value: 99.99% aluminium, 0.1-0.15 mm, pinched to a wire

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.aluminium.note: This is the vacuum-deposited aluminium behind the phosphor, and it is not the same part as the aluminium coating on the funnel wall behind the gun, which is a rear-facing mirror to recover light that would otherwise bounce around inside the tube. Both were often present; they are documented at peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.rear-al and both are fed from one roll of four-nines foil.

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.name: Phosphor-grade zinc sulphide
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.description: Zinc sulphide is the host crystal for all three P22 phosphors. It came from sphalerite, the zinc-iron sulphide ore, roasted in air to ZnO with the sulphur captured as SO2 for sulphuric acid. The ZnO was then converted back to high-purity ZnS, either by reacting with H2S or by reducing with hydrogen and re-sulphurising, because phosphor-grade sulphide has to be free of the iron and manganese that quench the emission.
inputs: hydrogen sulphide or hydrogen and sulphur

facts.label: Roast
facts.value: 700-850 degrees C, ZnS + 2O2 -> ZnO + SO2

facts.label: Phosphor calcine
facts.value: 900-1100 degrees C in a sealed quartz or alumina crucible under N2 with the activator

facts.label: Purification
facts.value: Fe and Mn kept below a few hundred ppm

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.note: It starts as a zinc mineral but it is bought by the phosphor industry, so it belongs to optics rather than metals. The zinc chain underneath it (sphalerite, the roast, the acid plant) stays metals, which is right: those are metallurgy.

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.name: Funnel glass batch, melted at 1400 degrees C
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.description: Funnel glass is a borosilicate with low alkali, formulated so that its thermal expansion matches the panel. The batch is silica sand, boric acid, soda ash, limestone and a little red lead or litharge as a fining agent, melted for tens of hours in a regenerative gas-fired tank furnace and then drawn into tubing.

facts.label: Melt temperature
facts.value: 1380-1500 degrees C

facts.label: Annealing
facts.value: lehr cooling 450 down to 20 degrees C over 10-20 hours

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.note: Borosilicate is the low-expansion family of glass: its main glass-formers are silica and boron trioxide and its coefficient of thermal expansion is about 3 x 10^-6 per K at 20 C, which is the order the figure here gives and the reason a funnel has to be formulated against the expansion of the panel it is sealed to. Not established: the 1380-1500 C melt temperature, the lehr cooling from 450 to 20 C over 10-20 hours, the regeneration gas firing, the red lead as fining agent, the forming of the funnel as drawn tubing, and the Toledo, Nemours and Tokyo works. A commercial lead borosilicate display-tube funnel glass was sold by the weight of its constituent oxides rather than by a published batch recipe.

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.name: Lead borosilicate sealing frit
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.description: The seal that makes a television tube possible, and a substance rather than an object: a glass with a recipe, printed onto the parts that have to become one. Lead oxide, silica, boric oxide and alkali are mixed with a water-soluble or organic vehicle into a paste and screen-printed through a 60-100 mesh onto the rim of the panel and the flange of the funnel, then dried and fired at 600-700 degrees C to drive the vehicle off and devitrify the band. Panel and funnel are then brought together in a continuous belt kiln, where the frit softens and fuses at 430-460 degrees C. Lead does three jobs: it drops the sealing temperature far below the point where the base glass would slump, it can be tuned to match the expansion of either glass, and its high atomic number soaks up the bremsstrahlung X-rays that 25 kV of beam current unavoidably produces inside the tube. The printed band has to be dimensionally exact - too narrow and it will not seal, too wide and it costs lead.

facts.label: PbO content
facts.value: roughly 24 wt% in the standard lead frit

facts.label: Print mesh
facts.value: 60-100 mesh for the seal band

facts.label: Band thickness
facts.value: 1-2 mm wet, shrinking to about 0.8-1.5 mm fired

facts.label: Devitrification
facts.value: 600-700 degrees C, in air, to remove the vehicle

facts.label: Seal temperature
facts.value: 430-460 degrees C in a continuous tunnel or belt kiln

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.note: Because the frit is a lead glass, a 1982 television tube is one of the largest deliberate lead-containing objects in the house. Real formulations ran from about a quarter to two thirds PbO depending on whether the set was sold as a colour tube with a separate shadow mask or a lower-cost monochrome-style lead frit, so treat 24% as representative, not universal. Modern seal bands use a photo-patterned photopaste so the frit only fires where it is needed, and modern sets moved to glass-to-glass bonding with the lead out of the frit entirely; the 1982 process was plain screen printing into a continuous belt kiln. Confidence on the chemistry is high; confidence on any particular tube's formulation is not, because the recipes were proprietary. Not established: the roughly 24 wt% PbO figure and the 88.05 keV lead K-absorption edge, the 60-100 mesh print, the 1-2 mm wet band thickness and the 430-460 C seal temperature. The 600-700 C devitrification appears elsewhere in this file under the panel glass node. The recipes were proprietary, so no particular tube's formulation can be given.

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.name: Panel glass, alkali-free
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.description: The panel is not the same glass as the funnel. It is alkali-free borosilicate with an expansion coefficient about a third lower than the funnel, so that when the panel is pressed against a mould during cooling it develops exactly the curvature the shadow mask geometry needs and stays there. Alkali is kept out because sodium and potassium diffuse and react with the phosphor layer on the inside face.

facts.label: Expansion
facts.value: about 3.0-3.5 x 10^-6 / K for the panel

facts.label: Forming
facts.value: pressed against a ribbed refractory block during annealing

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.note: The curved 13 inch panel of the period was not spherical. It used a spherical base plus a cylindrical or sphericon section, because a purely spherical screen needed too much mask curvature and too much deflection for its size.

peripheral.cassette.tape.coating.name: Coating line: doctor blade, orientation field, cure ovens
peripheral.cassette.tape.coating.description: A web of polyester film, a metre or more wide, unwinds and passes under a coating station where the magnetic dispersion is laid down in one or two passes by a doctor blade or a gravure roll, a few microns thick. It passes between magnets that align the acicular particles along the length of the film, then into an oven at 60-100 degrees C to drive off the solvent and cure the binder. A backing-coat station then applies the carbon-black anti-smear layer, and the whole web is slit to width.

facts.label: Web speed
facts.value: 300-900 m/min on a modern line; a 1982 line was 100-400 m/min

facts.label: Wet coating
facts.value: a few microns, shrinking to 1-2 microns of oxide

facts.label: Orientation field
facts.value: about 5-20 kA/m (roughly 100-250 Oe)

facts.label: Oven
facts.value: 60-100 degrees C, solvent flash and cure

facts.label: Passes
facts.value: one magnetic coat, plus a backing coat; sometimes a base coat

peripheral.cassette.tape.coating.note: Doctor blades (a blade wiping the web against a rubber roll) and gravure rolls (a patterned metal roll transferring a metered film) were both in use; gravure gave finer control and was the direction the industry moved. The solvent was recovered by condensing and distilling the oven exhaust, which is why a tape plant of the period smelled of toluene and had a distillation column.

peripheral.cassette.tape.slitting.name: Slitting to 1/8 inch
peripheral.cassette.tape.slitting.description: The coating line made a web a metre or more wide; it was then slit into 3.81 mm strips with rotary knives, tens of kilovolts of static keeping the thin film from clinging to the rollers. The slit tape was wound onto master reels, then onto cassette reels by a winding line that also cut it to length (45 m per side for a C-60), formed the leader, and inserted the hub.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: 45 m per side for a C-60, 135 m total; a C-90 is 45 m per side at a thinner gauge

facts.label: Gauge
facts.value: 9-12 microns of base film

peripheral.cassette.tape.slitting.note: A C-60 and a C-90 differ in length and gauge. A C-60 at 12 microns and a C-90 at 9 microns hold about the same total oxide per side, so the C-90 has to be made of a higher-output oxide (often cobalt-modified) to hold as much. The polyester base film is an ingredient of the slitting step. Not established: the coating-line web width, the rotary slitter knives, the static charge that holds the thin film off the rollers, and the 9-12 micron base gauge. The 3.81 mm strip width and the 45 m per side for a C-60 are the reliable parts.

peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb.plating.name: HASL: hot-tin-dipped tin-lead solder on the pads
peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb.plating.description: The board was dipped or dragged through a molten bath of 60/40 tin-lead, which left a solder film on the pads and bridged the copper under the mask. Immersion tin plating or gold-flash were also used, but a television of 1982 was overwhelmingly hot-tin-dipped. Tin from cassiterite, lead from galena, both of which are already in this tree.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: 60% tin / 40% lead, melt at 190 degrees C

facts.label: Solder mask over HASL
facts.value: mask printed before the dip, so the mask covers the throwaway copper

peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb.plating.note: The big tin solder smelters of the era were in Kuala Lumpur and Kuantan in Malaysia, on Bintan in Indonesia, and in Cornwall and Bolivia. The solder is the only tin-lead user of cassiterite in this branch; tin also went onto food cans, from the same ore.

peripheral.tv.aerial.whip.plating.name: Chrome-plate the whip rod
peripheral.tv.aerial.whip.plating.description: A telescopic rod plated in hard chrome over nickel, in several decorative layers so it could be extended and retracted thousands of times without wearing through. The chrome came from chromite ore, the same ore that made the chromium dioxide in a Type II cassette tape.

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: about 0.25-1 micron of hard chrome over nickel

facts.label: Chrome source
facts.value: chromic acid from chromite ore

peripheral.tv.aerial.whip.plating.note: Chrome plating is documented: it is a technique of electroplating a thin layer of chromium onto a metal object, the chromium layer can be decorative, provide corrosion resistance, facilitate cleaning, and increase surface hardness, and a less expensive substitute such as nickel may be used for aesthetic purposes. Not established: the 0.25-1 micron hard chrome thickness over a nickel underlayer, the several decorative layers, and that the plating was what let the rod be extended and retracted thousands of times without wearing through - hard chrome is hard but thin, so the endurance argument is plausible rather than demonstrated. The Japan and Taiwan attributions are not established either. The chromium here came from chromite, the same ore that made the chromium dioxide in a Type II cassette tape, which is a real convergence: one ore, two unrelated end uses.

peripheral.tv.cabinet.moulding.name: Injection mould the cabinet
peripheral.tv.cabinet.moulding.description: ABS pellets were dried, melted at 230-260 degrees C, injected into a nickel-chromium plated steel mould at 1000-2000 bar, held under pressure to pack, cooled on a water circuit and ejected. The cabinet was a single moulding with the speaker grille, the bezel ledges, the screw bosses and the airflow slots all integral; the front bezel was often a separate moulding in a different colour. A 13 inch set's mould ran 10,000 to a few hundred thousand shots.

facts.label: Melt temperature
facts.value: 230-260 degrees C

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 40-70 seconds

facts.label: Mould
facts.value: P20 or 1.2311 pre-hardened tool steel, nickel-plated

facts.label: Shrinkage
facts.value: 0.4-0.7% linear

facts.label: Mould steel
facts.value: P20 or 1.2311 pre-hardened tool steel, 30-35 HRC, electroless-nickel plated

peripheral.tv.cabinet.moulding.note: The mould is P20 tool steel with a nickel-chromium plating, held at 1000-2000 bar against the melt. Moulds are generally made from tool steels, and presses are rated by the clamping force they can exert. Not established: 1000-2000 bar injection pressure, the 230-260 C melt temperature, the 40-70 s cycle, P20 or 1.2311 at 30-35 HRC with electroless nickel, and the 0.4-0.7% linear shrinkage.

peripheral.tv.cabinet.screws.zinc-platin.name: Electroplate zinc onto the case screws
peripheral.tv.cabinet.screws.zinc-platin.description: Self-tapping screws into plastic bosses and a handful of machine screws into zinc-plated or black-oxide steel. Zinc plating is the cheapest corrosion protection for a small steel part and it came off the same zinc chain as everything else in this branch.

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: 5-15 microns zinc, plus a chromate conversion for a self-locking patch

facts.label: Bulkhead nut
facts.value: a nylon-insert or serrated nut to resist vibration

peripheral.tv.cabinet.screws.zinc-platin.note: Self-tapping screws into plastic bosses and a handful of machine screws into zinc-plated or black-oxide steel. Zinc plating is the cheapest corrosion protection for a small steel part, and it came off the same zinc chain as everything else in this branch: the electroplating bath is fed from sphalerite, it does not contain it, so the zinc is an ingredient here rather than a part of the screw.

peripheral.tv.tuner.can.zinc.name: Electroplate zinc onto the RF can
peripheral.tv.tuner.can.zinc.description: The stamped steel RF can was plated in a zinc sulphate or zinc chloride bath with an aluminium or steel anode, then often given a chromate passivation. Zinc plating is cheap corrosion protection and it is the same zinc industry as the CRT phosphor and the die-cast tuner body.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: acid sulphate or cyanide; sulphate was dominant by 1982 for non-electroplate

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: about 5-15 microns

peripheral.tv.tuner.can.zinc.note: The sphalerite reference is now an ingredient edge rather than a child, for the same reason as the case screws: a plating bath is fed from the zinc industry, it does not contain it.

peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.name: Evacuation, getter flash and exhaust tip
peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.description: The tube is evacuated on a manifold to better than 1e-6 mbar with a backing line of mechanical and diffusion pumps, tested with a spark-gap or ion gauge. Then the exhaust tip, a small tubulation drawn on the end of the funnel with a tantalum or aluminium-alloy cap welded over it, is opened with a glass break or an RF induction heater. The get, a flash of barium-titanium-palladium inside the neck, absorbs any remaining gas and then fixes a mirror-like barium film on the tube wall. The tip is then crushed flat and sealed.
inputs: high-voltage feedthrough for the anode button

facts.label: Base pressure
facts.value: 1e-6 to 1e-7 torr

facts.label: Getter
facts.value: Ba-Ti-Pd flake, flashed by RF induction

facts.label: Exhaust tip cap
facts.value: tantalum, or an aluminium-magnesium alloy, welded on

facts.label: Pump combination
facts.value: rotary or water-ring roughing plus an oil diffusion or BHK mercury pin pump

peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.note: No source was found for any of the figures here. The sequence described is the standard one for a vacuum tube or envelope - evacuate, leak-test, open the exhaust tip, flash the getter, then seal - and a barium getter that is flashed by heating and deposits a mirror film on the wall is a real and widely used mechanism. Not established: the 1e-6 to 1e-7 torr base pressure, the Ba-Ti-Pd flake composition and its RF induction flash, the tantalum or aluminium-magnesium tip cap, the mercury (BHK) pin pump as opposed to a diffusion pump, the spark-gap or ion gauge, and the St. Louis, Taiwan and Japan works. Barium for the getter is not specific to the get itself: the same alkaline-earth chain feeds the cathode coating, the speaker ferrite and the getter, and the three are separate buyers of the same ore.

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.blackening.name: Blacken the anode with a sooty flame
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.blackening.description: The anode block and the inside of the funnel near the neck are flame-blacked with a sooty acetylene flame so that any stray electrons are absorbed rather than bouncing around the tube. Carbon black, the same pigment as in the cabinet and in a car's tyres, does the job here.
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.blackening.note: Carbon black is documented as the pigment made by the incomplete combustion of coal tar, vegetable matter or petroleum products, and a blackened surface to suppress stray emission is a real mechanism. Not established: acetylene as the sooting flame, that the inside of the funnel near the neck was blackened as well as the anode block, and that the blackening was done to absorb stray electrons rather than for heat or light control. Tube makers also graphitised the anode by firing in a reducing atmosphere, which is a different route to the same result, and this node describes only the flame route.

peripheral.tv.crt.mask.etch.name: Photoetch of the slots
peripheral.tv.crt.mask.etch.description: The flat sheet is cleaned, coated with photoresist, exposed through a master plate that defines every slot, developed, and etched. Ferric chloride is the etchant of the period for steel. After etching the sheet is washed, stress-relieved by heating, then pressed into a spherical section on a matched former, and the round holes open into slots as it bends.

facts.label: Etchant
facts.value: ferric chloride, or nitric plus sulphuric acid

facts.label: Forming
facts.value: pressed to a radius about 1.5x the panel face radius

facts.label: Stress relief
facts.value: annealed after etching so the foil does not spring

peripheral.tv.crt.mask.etch.note: Electroformed nickel masks and bimetallic masks came later and solved the thermal expansion mismatch between steel mask and panel; a 1982 tube used a single low-carbon steel mask whose expansion roughly matched the panel glass.

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.print.name: Print and fire the internal phosphor screen
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.print.description: Three slurries are laid down in turn: red, then green, then blue, each through a fine nylon mesh onto the inside of the panel, each registered to the last to a few tens of microns. The mesh, not a photo-emulsion, defines the dots; a photographic stencil fixes the screen area and the black border. Each slurry carries 10-30% by weight of a finely ground low-melting glass frit, because without a glassy binder the phosphor dust would wipe off the panel at the first wipe. The printed panel then goes into an exhausted conveyor oven at 430-450 degrees C for 30-60 minutes: the organic vehicle decomposes and burns off completely, which is why the tunnel has to be exhausted, and the frit flows and wets the phosphor grains into a solid, adherent, moisture-resistant layer. Under 400 degrees leaves carbon in the layer; over 460 starts to attack the phosphor and shift the colour. Some lines ran the blue under nitrogen to protect it. Screen frits of this era could contain lead or barium; the formulations were proprietary.

facts.label: Mesh
facts.value: about 200-400 mesh

facts.label: Registration
facts.value: better than 25 microns between colour prints

facts.label: Vehicle
facts.value: PVA plus a plasticiser, burnt out in the firing

facts.label: Firing
facts.value: 430-450 degrees C, 30-60 minutes, in air and exhausted

facts.label: Firing atmosphere
facts.value: air; some lines ran N2 to protect the blue phosphor

facts.label: Frit in the slurry
facts.value: 10-30% by weight of finely ground low-melting glass, lead-bearing or barium-bearing

children.name: Three-roll mill
children.description: The phosphor slurry is refined on a three-roll (three-mill) gap mill: the rollers set a gap of a few microns and shear the agglomerates down so that the particle size distribution is tight. Screen printing needs a narrow size distribution or the dots print with a rough edge and the resolution falls off.

facts.label: Gap
facts.value: a few microns, set by feel across the roll

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: 2-6 microns for screen-printing grade phosphor

children.note: No source was found for the three-roll mill in this position. A three-roll gap mill is a standard machine for dispersing a pigment paste and breaking agglomerates by shear between rollers, and a narrow particle-size distribution is a real requirement for a fine phosphor dot, so the machine is a reasonable choice. Not established: the roll gap of a few microns set by feel, the 2-6 micron particle size quoted for screen-printing grade phosphor, and that a three-roll mill rather than a ball mill, a colloid mill or a bead mill was what a CRT phosphor line actually ran. The gap figure in particular is a shop-floor rule of thumb rather than a specification.

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.print.note: Printing and firing are one operation on the panel and are kept as one node, because the frit only becomes a binder in the furnace: you cannot specify one without the other. The three-roll mill that refines the slurry is a child because it is capital equipment standing beside the line; the frit and the vehicle are ingredients and are not.

peripheral.cassette.tape.coating.backing.name: Backing coat: carbon black for the leader and anti-smear
peripheral.cassette.tape.coating.backing.description: On the back of the magnetic coating was a sub-micron layer of extra pigment and carbon black. It did two things: it gave the visible leader tape (the clear or white strip at the start of a cassette) its colour and its opacity so a deck could find it, and it suppressed print-through, where a signal on one layer of the wound tape magnetises the layer next to it and comes back as a ghost. Carbon black, again, from petroleum coke.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 0.5-2 microns

facts.label: Leader
facts.value: about 1.5 m at each end, opaque to a reflective tape-position sensor

peripheral.cassette.tape.coating.backing.note: The carbon black comes as an ingredient, out of the petroleum-coke chain.

peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.barium.name: Barium getter foil
peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.barium.description: The getter is a thin foil strip of barium, titanium and palladium powder bonded with a glass frit in a nickel tube. When RF-heated it explodes in a burst of vacuum, sprays barium across the neck, and the barium burns and sticks to the glass as a mirror film. That film is the biggest vapour getter in the tube and turns residual gas into metal. Barium metal was made by reducing barite (BaSO4) with carbon or aluminium.

facts.label: Barite
facts.value: BaSO4, 4.5+ tonnes per m3, mined open pit and underground

facts.label: Barium metal
facts.value: Al reduction at 1100-1200 degrees C, then vacuum distillation

peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.barium.note: It sits near the ferrite and the barite because the element is the same, but the getter is a barium-titanium-palladium foil, not a ferrite.

peripheral.tv.crt.mask.steel.bf.name: Smelt the iron and blow it in a basic oxygen furnace
peripheral.tv.crt.mask.steel.bf.description: Sintered iron ore, coke and limestone are charged to a blast furnace at 1500-1600 degrees C. Hot metal comes out at about 4% carbon, is blown in a BOF to 0.05-0.1%, and is continuously cast into slabs that go to the hot strip mill.

facts.label: BOF
facts.value: 0.1-0.6% residual C, 25-30 minutes

facts.label: Slab
facts.value: 200-300 mm thick, 10-30 tonnes

peripheral.tv.crt.mask.steel.bf.note: Blast furnaces work by chemical reduction, carbon monoxide converting iron oxides to elemental iron, and blowing oxygen through molten pig iron lowers its carbon content to low-carbon steel; a modern converter takes a charge of up to 400 tons and makes steel in under 40 minutes. Not established: 1500-1600 C in the furnace, the 4-4.5% carbon of the hot metal, the 0.1-0.6% residual carbon, the 200-300 mm slab, and the Gary, Duisburg and Kawasaki attributions.

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.roast-s.name: Roast, sinter and smelt the lead concentrate
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.roast-s.description: The whole lead chain in one furnace hall. Concentrate is roasted in a fluid-bed roaster to litharge, PbO, with the SO2 sent to a contact plant for sulphuric acid; the litharge is mixed with sinter, coke and limestone and charged to a blast furnace that produces crude lead at about 1250 degrees C and 1100-1250 degrees C of shaft temperature. The crude is drossed and electrolytically refined to 99.99% Pb, then converted back to pure white PbO for the frit. The economics were dominated by the acid plant and by how much silver the Parkesine dross carried.

facts.label: Roaster
facts.value: fluid bed, 600-750 degrees C, PbS + 3/2 O2 -> PbO + SO2

facts.label: Sinter
facts.value: roasted concentrate sintered on a Dwight-Lloyd grate, 1200-1400 degrees C

facts.label: Blast furnace
facts.value: shaft at 1100-1250 degrees C, crude lead at about 1250 degrees C, 3-5% by mass in the metal

facts.label: Refining
facts.value: anode slime carries the silver; electrolytic tankhouse to 99.99% Pb

facts.label: To litharge
facts.value: the refined Pb is oxidised back to PbO in a reverberatory or fluid-bed converter

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.roast-s.note: Primary lead production is documented as a sinter blast-furnace route: concentrated ore is sintered with iron, silica and limestone fluxes and coke, reduced in a blast furnace, the bullion is copper-drossed and drossed, the Parkes process is used to separate silver and gold from lead, and the metal is then refined, with the Betterton-Kroll process among the pyrometallurgical routes named. That much is the sequence this node describes. Not established: the fluid-bed roaster at 600-750 C and the PbS oxidation equation, the Dwight-Lloyd grate and the 1200-1400 C sinter, the 1100-1250 C shaft temperature and the 1250 C crude-lead figure, the 3-5% silver in the metal, the conversion of refined Pb back to white PbO in a reverberatory or fluid-bed converter, and the Herculaneum, Midland and Port Pirie works. The claimed dominance of the acid plant and of the silver in the dross is a plausible industrial argument, not a measurement.

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.so2.name: Convert sulphur dioxide to sulphuric acid
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.so2.description: The roaster's off-gas is cleaned, converted to SO3 on a vanadium pentoxide catalyst at about 450 degrees C and absorbed in 98% acid in a double-contact plant. It is the reason a 1982 zinc smelter had an acid plant as large as the roaster.

facts.label: Contact
facts.value: V2O5 catalyst, 450-480 degrees C

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.so2.note: Industrial SO2 oxidation is at about 420-620 C over vanadium(V) oxide catalysts, typically around 450 C, and zinc is refined by froth flotation, roasting and electrowinning, so the roaster off-gas really is a SO2 source. Not established: the 98-99% acid absorption, and the claim that a 1982 zinc smelter's acid plant was as large as the roaster.

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.seal-kiln.name: Continuous belt kiln
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.seal-kiln.description: A continuous refractory belt kiln, with a jig that aligns the printed panel rim to the funnel flange as the two travel through the firing zone where the frit melts and fuses. The seal is judged visually, by how far the heated frit bulges past its own edge. The tube is then helium leak tested on a separate manifold before it ever goes near the vacuum pumps, and that test is a gauge on a manifold rather than part of the kiln.

facts.label: Zone temperature
facts.value: 430-460 degrees C peak

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: tens of minutes

facts.label: Leak criterion
facts.value: 10^-7 mbar l/s helium

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.seal-kiln.note: Ion-pump or penning-gauge helium leak testing at that sensitivity was standard practice; the exact acceptance spec varies by plant, which is why the confidence here is low. The node is the kiln: the leak test used to share the title with it, and two different objects do not belong in one name.

peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.rear-al.name: Aluminium coating on the funnel wall
peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.rear-al.description: A separate aluminium mirror, vapour-deposited on the inside of the funnel behind the gun, intended to bounce stray light back towards the phosphor and raise light output. It is distinct from the phosphor back layer, which is where the black level comes from. Modern practice replaced it with a black internal coating on the neck to absorb stray light instead, and moved efficiency to the phosphor and to tinted faceplate glass.
peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.rear-al.note: Both the aluminium funnel coating and the phosphor aluminium layer are real and were often both present. An aluminium-backed faceplate is a reasonable description of the phosphor back layer, and the funnel coating is the separate, less discussed item. Both mirrors behind a tube come from the same roll of four-nines foil.

peripheral.why-rf.tv-loses-75-ohm.name: Signal-level margin between a modulator and a transmitter
peripheral.why-rf.tv-loses-75-ohm.description: A broadcast TV station transmitted tens of kilowatts; a C64 modulator put out about a milliwatt. The set had to be tuned by hand, and reception quality was a function of the modulator's output impedance matching the aerial input. Anyone who ever moved the TV or unplugged the aerial lead knows how marginal this was.
peripheral.why-rf.tv-loses-75-ohm.note: Quantitative comparison of received signal levels is reconstructed from general receiver-sensitivity reasoning rather than from a measurement of a specific 1.1902-type modulator.

peripheral.why-rf.modern-comparison.name: Later video connectors: the 1702 DIN and the C128 RGBI
peripheral.why-rf.modern-comparison.description: Commodore's own 1702 monitor took a composite luma-and-blank input over a 5-pin DIN, and in 1985-86 Commodore adopted the DE-9 connector used by the C128's RGBI monitors, which carried separate red, green and blue analogue signals on pins 5, 6, 7 with no modulation at all. There was still no standard, which is why the C128 ended up with a proprietary DIN-8 video connector rather than a DE-15.
peripheral.why-rf.modern-comparison.note: The 1702 and the C128 RGBI monitors are real objects but they are not upstream of a 1982 C64, so they do not belong on a supply line.
